Reviews and verification evidence must identify the source revision they assess. New changes must invalidate or refresh relevant conclusions. Successful tool completion must not be reported as passing checks, review approval, or merge success without observed evidence.

When a feature completes, automatically remove all harness-created worktrees and local branches associated with that feature across every involved repository, including task and integration worktrees/branches. Retain transcripts, commit identities, PR/review links, and the historical ownership records after the local Git resources are removed.

Before cleanup, verify resource ownership and integration evidence and stop any remaining writers. Cleanup must not discard uncommitted work or unintegrated commits, or remove unrelated user resources. Record each result; expose failures and a retry path instead of silently reporting successful cleanup. Paused features retain the worktrees needed for continuation.

Features must always use a feature branch in each affected repository. Task PRs target that feature branch. The feature coordinator chooses whether related tasks share a PR or have separate PRs; one PR per task is not required. Open the final feature PR to main only once the feature implementation is complete, never as an early task-delivery path. The final feature PRs remain linked to the same feature and its task/group PR history.

Distinguish implementation completion, final PR delivery, and cleanup in execution state and the UI. Implementation completion permits the final feature PR to main; review/fix/check and Auto-Merge policies still govern its merge. Keep needed worktrees and branches while final delivery is pending. Run feature-completion cleanup after final integration is verified across the affected repositories, and show cleanup failures explicitly. This sequencing preserves the required branch while its final PR is open.

Every task must document its associated current worktrees, branches and PRs so the user can easily find where its work lives. Show the repository, worktree path, branch name and PR link on the task, including each relevant repository for cross-repository work. Grouped-task PRs must be linked from every covered task. Preserve historical associations after cleanup and distinguish removed or closed resources from current ones.

Standalone issues use an isolated task branch and worktree and open PRs directly to main. They do not require a feature branch. Preserve configured review/fix/check and Auto-Merge policy and show branch/worktree/PR links on the issue. Tasks belonging to features retain the existing feature-branch delivery flow.

After verified merge of an issue to main, automatically clean up its harness-owned worktrees and local branches. Retain transcripts, artifacts, GitHub links and complete work history. Preserve unintegrated work and show cleanup failure/retry state under GIT-07.

Agents may automatically force-push their own task branches, including after a rebase. Force-pushing feature branches requires explicit user approval; branches outside an agent-owned task branch must not receive automatic force-push authority. Never force-push to main. This prohibition applies regardless of Auto-Merge settings, package/tool configuration or an approval for another operation, and must cover equivalent forced updates to the main ref. Existing repository access controls and branch protections remain in effect; approval does not authorize bypassing them. Record permitted force-pushes, approvals, denials and outcomes in the linked task/feature and agent history.

Before a force-push, resolve the actual repository, remote and destination ref, check task-branch ownership and effective branch protection, and validate any required approval against that concrete operation. Use an explicit expected remote revision with force-with-lease or an equivalent guarded update so concurrent remote changes cause refusal and reconciliation rather than overwrite. Unknown ownership must not qualify for automatic authority. Enforce the main prohibition for harness-dispatched Git operations, including forced refspecs and equivalent invocation forms. Define preflight, shell/tool enforcement and approval-binding mechanics, preserving the absolute main prohibition under GIT-13.

For a feature spanning multiple repositories, all final feature PRs must pass their required checks and reviews before any final PR is merged. Once every final PR is ready, merge them in dependency order. Apply each repository’s effective Auto-Merge, review and approval policies; readiness does not grant authority to merge when that authority is disabled or awaiting approval. Track each repository’s delivery result and the feature’s overall delivery history.

Resolve routine merge conflicts autonomously and continue delivery without notifying the user or requesting routine conflict-resolution approval. Concurrent agents working in the same repository are expected to cause conflicts; the coordinator must reconcile their changes while preserving the approved feature requirements. Conflict resolution does not waive required checks, reviews, repository merge authority or the prohibition on force-pushing main. If a merge fails in an unusual way that the coordinator cannot resolve, pause the affected delivery and dependent work and notify the user with the failure, attempts and evidence. Independent work continues; ordinary recoverable conflicts are recorded in history without a user notification.

A feature is complete once all of its final feature PRs are verified as merged into main across the affected repositories. Track releases and deployments separately, retaining links to the feature, repositories, revisions and delivery history. A pending, approval-waiting or failed release or deployment must not keep the merged feature open. Release and deployment actions retain their separate configured authority under DELIVERY-09. Feature completion triggers the required cleanup of harness-owned worktrees and local branches under GIT-06–09; retain the feature’s history and artifacts and expose cleanup outcomes separately.

Auto-Merge and mandatory independent review default to on, with project and repository overrides. Auto-Merge off stops before merge. Configured GitHub automated reviews satisfy mandatory review; repositories without working automation use an independent in-app reviewer. Both sources feed the fix cycle, and every actionable finding must be resolved. Deployments and release publishing have independent inherited policies under DELIVERY-09, both defaulting to Ask me. Force-push authority follows GIT-13: automatic only for agent-owned task branches, approval for feature branches and never main. Review-source discovery and completion follow the architecture contract; native qualification, other destructive Git authority and protected-branch enforcement remain implementation work.

History retention must include failures, retries, interrupted sessions, superseded plans, previous coordinators, and abandoned branches where they explain the work. History search and filters must support at least actor, event type, work identity, repository, and time or session context.

Every project must have a local artifact store for screenshots, files, reports and other work outputs. Agents must be able to save, discover and read artifacts through first-class tools and share stable references with other agents and humans. Humans must be able to add and inspect files through the UI. Artifacts must retain explicit links to their originating project and, where applicable, feature and task, with navigation from that work to the artifact and back. Later reuse must preserve those origin links.

Give each artifact stable identity and metadata for name, media type, size, tags, creation time, producing agent/session, feature/task and relevant repository revision. Preserve source relationships and versions instead of silently overwriting referenced evidence. Show attachments in conversations, task/feature history and a searchable project Artifacts view, with image/text previews and file open/export controls.

Store artifact contents as local files managed outside disposable worktrees, SQLite metadata and graph provenance links. Publish complete files atomically and preserve references across restart, agent handoff and Git cleanup. Feature completion must not delete its artifacts when branches and worktrees are removed. No separate object-storage server or cloud account is required.

Artifact access must honor project scope and effective tool policy, including read-only reviewers. Supply bounded previews or file references to agents rather than inserting every file into model context. Define storage location, quotas and deletion behavior in Settings; retain artifacts until explicitly deleted under ART-05 and show disk/write failures. Include contents and metadata in backup/restore and avoid silently deleting referenced evidence.

Keep project artifacts until explicitly deleted. Automatic expiration or cleanup must be disabled by default; artifact age, feature completion, worktree cleanup and storage pressure must not silently remove retained files. Storage limits must produce visible status rather than implicit deletion.

title: 13 Primary chat interface
intro: The workspace conversation is the face of the product. Project management, source control, routing, and knowledge remain available around it, without turning the opening screen into a metrics dashboard.
blocks: Figure 2 Approved Chat layout with Current and Chat History tabs integrated header and floating completion cards

Chat is the primary app-wide interface. Place existing navigation on the left, the active workspace coordinator conversation in the center, and a right sidebar with Current first and Chat History second. Current is selected initially. Overview remains specific to the selected project. Do not replace the sidebar with a conversation dropdown.

The center conversation must support a persistent composer, readable messages and tool or result summaries, and links to the work being discussed. The initial state must invite a conversation with workspace-wide scope. Keep the integrated Workspace coordinator header; omit the redundant conversation-name row and Across your projects status strip because Current supplies that information. Align the plus attachment button, model/tier and effort controls with Send along the bottom of the workspace input. Below its border, show All projects followed by the pinned model on the left and the send keyboard hint on the right; omit redundant Workspace coordinator text. Preserve usable wrapping at narrower sizes. Every composer retains attachments under UI-08 and routing/effort under UI-10.

The right sidebar must provide Current and Chat History tabs without disrupting the conversation. Current shows app-wide Needs you, Working and Recently completed, with project labels and direct links to affected work. Chat History shows prior workspace conversations, the active selection, search and useful date grouping. Keep New Chat in the persistent center header beside Coordinator instructions, available with either tab selected. Tab changes and navigation preserve the active session, per-chat draft, attachments and relevant scroll positions; session selection restores the correct transcript. Feature coordinator conversations remain attached to their features.
The user must be able to leave chat to inspect a detailed screen and return without losing the conversation, its session selection, or its connection to ongoing work.

Coordinator role instructions, workspace scope, and relevant context must be inspectable. Detailed routing configuration must remain in Settings, while request attribution and cost may be inspected when useful.

Place the app-wide Approvals destination directly below Chat in the left navigation, with an all-project inbox and project filtering. Activity belongs inside the project-specific Overview as a section with filters and full history, rather than a separate left-navigation destination. Keep Intelligence navigation collapsible without losing access to its screens.

Use the approved Workspace coordinator / Overview visual language across every page and secondary view: warm neutral surfaces, bordered content groups, consistent type, spacing and quieter secondary actions. Integrate each page header into its primary content pane, with one continuous outer border and a divider into the body; do not use a detached full-width header card. Secondary panes start alongside the header. Place inner sidebars on the right for Approvals, Knowledge entries/documents, Dreaming run history and Databases. Complete the same grouping and header treatment for Repositories, Agents, Artifacts, Knowledge, Dreaming and all Database states/views. Overview and Features summary values and labels sit inline with matching baseline, size and spacing directly beneath the integrated header. Left-align the version and update message at the bottom of the left sidebar. Preserve existing capabilities and navigation/selection/filter/scroll behavior.

The approved UI reference is docs/planning/ui-reference.md and the revision 08 screen gallery. These define presentation alongside the numbered requirements; browser prototype evidence does not complete native implementation acceptance.

title: 14 Detailed UI workspaces
intro: The reviewed project, feature, repository, review and notification workspaces remain the baseline. Memory, knowledge and lessons are consolidated into one tagged Knowledge workspace. Chat remains the primary entry point alongside direct management screens.
blocks: Figure 3 Approved feature board with integrated header repository scope and its attached coordinator conversation
Oversee projects and active or paused work, then open a project or feature directly. Include archived project browsing and a distinct permanent-deletion action.

Search, filter, prioritize, create, and edit features; inspect member repositories, active coordination, decisions, and recent activity. Show and control per-project keep-working mode and its current selection/start activity.

Kanban board, requirements and acceptance, code changes by repository, history, context, and a persistent feature coordinator conversation. Start, Continue, Pause, and redirect controls remain connected to execution state.

Create, search, filter, prioritize and inspect tasks, including standalone issues with no feature. Task details expose execution controls, agent conversation/history, evidence and current Git locations.
Membership, local paths and remotes, branch and worktree state, changes, PRs, and indexing or semantic coverage.
Inspect coordinators, workers, sessions, assignment state, current work, errors, and attributed project history.
One searchable workspace for memory, knowledge and lessons, distinguished by tags; shared inspection/editing, evidence, confidence, scope, freshness, revisions and learning lifecycle controls.
Project files and screenshots shared by humans and agents; browse, search, preview, attach and inspect provenance.
Consolidation runs, instruction versions, budgets, reports, journals and unresolved conflicts; link changes back to the unified Knowledge workspace.
Actionable conflicts with evidence and affected work, and a global notification inbox with deep links and independent read state.

A full Settings workspace for routing, MCP servers, GitHub, jobs, CodeGraph operations, database connections, tool permissions, skills, and preferences; usage and costs remain a separate reporting screen.
Manage language packs and harness packages from Settings; inspect installation, updates, contributions, effective access, approvals, compatibility and diagnostics.

Use the CodeGraph repository home and its navigation as the baseline: overview, nodes, health, reviews, internal code projects, node-type browsing, linked entities and source. Database schema navigation and additional graph views remain to be refined.
Inspect analysis results, findings, evidence, source revisions, review history, and related work; distinct from the knowledge conflict queue.
Manage reusable conventions and skills, scope and applicability, versions, activation, and how agents receive them. A wiki interface is not required.
Inspect operation status and detailed logs, failures, attempts, and recovery actions.
First-class destination near Settings for entirely local, offline, version-matched system/UI documentation and extension-authoring guides, searchable by humans and agents.

Every long-running operation must expose current state, progress where meaningful, cancellation or pause where supported, and recoverable errors. Empty, loading, offline, partial-data, failed, and stale-data states must be designed rather than represented as fabricated success or zero values.

Keyboard navigation, readable focus states, screen-reader labels, text scaling, accessible status changes, and large histories must be supported. Resize behavior must preserve the conversation and essential controls. Theme customization and exact native pane sizing remain open; the shared visual direction follows UI-15.

Every chat input must accept images and files through a selection dialog, drag-and-drop and paste. Apply this to workspace, feature, issue and every other interactive agent chat composer. Attachments must accompany the correct message and remain accessible from its conversation history; image inspection follows ROUTE-13. Use a plus-only attachment button with an accessible name and tooltip explaining that it attaches images or files.

Show pending attachments with filenames and image previews where supported; allow removal before sending and preserve them with per-chat drafts. Store durable copies and stable attachment references, retaining conversation and applicable project/feature/task provenance through the artifact system. Workspace attachments without a project retain their conversation scope until associated with work. Define file formats, size limits, clipboard handling and extraction; show unsupported or failed processing rather than pretending unread content was analyzed. Preserve original attachments through context compaction and provider changes.

Every chat input must include a selector populated with configured router tiers and available named models under ROUTE-19, plus a separate effort selector under ROUTE-20. Tier Max, High, Mid and Low precede the named model group; Open Router Auto selects the OpenRouter automatic route directly. Selection and effort persist for the chat and are shared between Home and its sidebar. Tier allocation pins its resolved model until changed or replaced by eligible failover under ROUTE-14–15. All requests still pass through the router and respect permissions and required capabilities.

The revision 08 screenshots illustrate the approved layout, navigation and sample interactions under UI-14/15. Exact native color values, typography metrics and pane widths remain implementation details within that visual direction. Prototype screenshots do not substitute for native acceptance.

The updated UI study 05 preserves the chat-first layout and existing workspaces while adding standalone issues, unified tagged Knowledge, repository and schema exploration, health/reviews, agents and resources, project artifacts, approvals, scheduled jobs, comprehensive Settings, and usage/cache reporting. Model selectors and file/image attachment interactions are represented in chat composers. All data, inference and external operations are simulated locally; this is a browser-based design reference for the future native egui product, not its implementation. Newly added layouts and proposed interaction details remain subject to user review. The requirements interview has resumed at the user’s request.

Provide Help as a first-class menu/navigation item near Settings. It must open a searchable documentation workspace and remain readily accessible from the main interface. Every screen and Settings section must include a contextual Help link that opens its relevant local documentation topic.

Document every aspect of the working system, including every UI screen, action and setting; project/repository/work/agent workflows; planning, approvals and delivery; routing and context; knowledge and skills; indexing and graph/schema exploration; jobs, containers and integrations; artifacts, storage and lifecycle; and diagnostics, recovery, permissions and limitations. Explain actual behavior, defaults, configuration scope and practical use. Documentation is a core product capability and must be maintained with the functionality it describes.

Document all supported extensibility points and how to create plugins/add-ins, including harness packages and semantic language packs. Provide developer guidance for SDKs, manifests, protocols, tools/commands, workflows/events, context/instruction extensions, native UI contributions and router/provider adapters where supported. Cover prerequisites, development/build/test, packaging, installation/configuration, permissions and approvals, compatibility/versioning, updates, troubleshooting and rollback, with usable examples. Distinguish supported contracts from unimplemented or unsupported capabilities.

Make system and extension documentation accessible to agents through first-class search/read tools so coordinators, workers and read-only reviewers can learn and use the system they operate. Humans and agents must access the same maintained documentation. Documentation retrieval follows configured tool permissions and must not grant authority or override user directions. Agent access must cover UI behavior as well as tools and extensibility, not just tool schema descriptions.

Help must live entirely locally and offline, bundled and versioned alongside the app and installed add-ons. Match app documentation to the installed app version and add-on documentation to the installed add-on version. Human browsing/search and agent documentation search/read tools must operate on this local content without requiring a network connection, hosted documentation service or remote search fallback.

Use stable topic identifiers and contextual links from errors; screen and Settings-section Help links are required under HELP-01. Let agents retrieve bounded passages with topic/version references instead of injecting the entire manual into each session. Review documentation coverage and examples alongside capability changes, and expose missing, stale or unavailable documentation. Exact local authoring format, search/indexing, packaging/update mechanics and documentation checks remain to specify; offline-only content and version matching are confirmed under HELP-05.

title: 15 Context memory knowledge lessons and rules
blocks: Memory, knowledge and lessons are one connected Knowledge system, differentiated by tags in a single workspace. Their useful metadata remains: claims retain evidence and confidence; decisions retain rationale; lessons retain applicability and learning history. CodeGraph already models Lesson as a KnowledgeKind with additional learning lifecycle state. The rewrite preserves needed behavior without inheriting separate catalogs. Project/shared scope is independent of category tags.

The user must have one Knowledge workspace consolidating memory, knowledge and lessons, differentiated by tags. It must support inspection, tag search and filtering, manual creation and editing, lifecycle changes, and source evidence. Agents must use the same connected knowledge system through tools.

Memory must represent entities and atomic claims with predicates, values, scope, evidence, author or agent provenance, confidence, timestamps, and revision history. Conflicting observations must remain inspectable until resolved; confidence must not be presented as proof.

Knowledge must support goals, decisions, constraints, facts, gotchas, attempts, architecture notes, and lessons, with active, superseded, or retracted lifecycle states as appropriate. Verification must record the evidence and source revision used, and later source changes must be able to mark entries stale. Each decision records who made it. A decision the user made or approved, including one approved in chat and recorded by an agent, names the user as its origin; only a decision an agent made on its own is marked autonomous. Autonomous decisions stay visible for reading and never ask the user to acknowledge them; the review queue under REVIEW-01 holds only conflicts an agent cannot resolve.

Lessons and rules must be visible with their origin, applicability, recurrence, challenges, and relationship to the work where they were learned or used. Agents must be able to retrieve and manage them through tools.

The lesson lifecycle must distinguish candidate evidence, proposed rules, effective rules, and rejected proposals. Human instructions, review-derived lessons, and repeated corrections must retain their distinct provenance; recurrence alone must not be treated as proof of effectiveness. A rule’s origin decides how it takes effect. A rule from the user’s own instruction or review, given directly or relayed by an agent with the user’s words attached, takes effect immediately without approval; it is the user’s own edit under EVAL-05 and is monitored under EVAL-07. A lesson inferred by an agent, subagent or automated reviewer stays candidate evidence until it recurs across a configured number of distinct source events, then takes effect automatically without approval and is monitored under EVAL-07 like any other change that takes effect without approval under EVAL-05. No rule asks the user for approval; the user may promote a candidate early, or challenge or retire any rule, at any time. Taking effect is not proof that a rule works. Eval evidence under EVAL-08 may show whether a lesson rule is effective.

Rule delivery must be inspectable: the app must record which relevant rules and revisions were supplied to a session. It must expose whether a lesson has been addressed in code, instructions, a skill, documentation, or a test, and surface unmatched or unlearned evidence where useful.

General lessons must be available across projects automatically without manual sharing or promotion for each project. Project-specific knowledge and conventions must remain scoped to their project. Shared lessons must retain their origin and applicability; automatic availability does not make every lesson relevant to every task. Project-scoped content must remain scoped in agent retrieval and context assembly, including when dreaming consolidates it.

Consolidate memory, knowledge and lessons into one Knowledge system and workspace, differentiated by tags rather than independent catalogs. Preserve identity, evidence, relationships, revisions and applicable learning metadata without duplicating the same item across categories. Scope remains a separate property: a lesson tag alone must not share project-specific content. Human and agent tools must support the same tagging and scoped retrieval operations.

Knowledge search must let an agent bound one page of results by a token budget, filled with the best-ranked claims first. The budget sets the page size and must not make any claim unreachable: the remaining claims stay available on later pages. The default budget and the largest budget a caller may pass must be configurable, inherited Workspace then Project; a caller may pass its own budget on a call within the allowed range. A person searching in the app is not limited by the budget.

Context assembly must combine the work brief, current plan, instructions, relevant code and graph results, scoped knowledge, applicable lessons, prior evidence, and handover state within a deliberate token budget. It must preserve provenance instead of indiscriminately replaying all repository content and chat history.

A session must record its instruction revisions, retrieved context sources, important omissions or truncation, and routing metadata sufficiently to explain what information the agent acted on. Context updates and summaries must preserve unresolved constraints and decisions.

Resolve enforced permissions and explicit user directions before repository guidance. Applicable repository instructions override default role instructions. Resolve repository conflicts by nearest directory first, only within its subtree; at one directory AGENTS.md overrides CLAUDE.md, whose nonconflicting instructions still apply. Preserve nonconflicting ancestor rules. Discover only authorized instruction roots, retain exact source digests/applicability in each effective context and reconcile material unresolved conflicts visibly. Same-level ambiguity cannot grant authority or silently affect another repository.

When an agent reaches 80% of the active model’s maximum context, the harness must automatically compact its working context and continue without user intervention. Preserve the complete original transcript and the same logical agent identity and work relationships. Compaction must not replace or truncate the stored transcript; record the compaction and resulting continuation in the agent’s session history. Any compaction inference must use the router.

Measure context against the actual routed model/endpoint limit, including instructions, tool schemas, messages and tool results with appropriate modality accounting. Reserve response/tool headroom and check request size before dispatch, including after model changes. Compaction must preserve current requirements, plan state, user directions, unresolved decisions and relevant evidence/artifact references. Unknown limits, oversized single inputs and failed compaction need visible bounded recovery rather than silent truncation or loss of work.

Automatically load applicable repository and subdirectory AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md instructions. Instructions closest to the target files override conflicting ancestor instructions within that subtree. At the same directory level AGENTS.md wins conflicts; CLAUDE.md adds nonconflicting guidance. Repository instructions override default role instructions. User directions and enforced permissions remain above all file instructions. Preserve path applicability across multiple directories/repositories; files cannot grant tool authority.

Exact knowledge import/export, entity merge/unmerge, retention, classification of general versus project-specific content, and rule-promotion policy need capability-level review. General lessons are shared automatically; project-specific knowledge and conventions remain project-scoped under KNOW-07. These are not blanket exclusions: the selected CodeGraph core must be assessed and every required capability represented before implementation scope is approved.

title: 16 Dreaming review queue and notifications
blocks: Dreaming must consolidate and maintain memory, knowledge, and lessons with visible runs and outcomes. The user must be able to inspect what was considered, what changed, what was proposed, and what remains unresolved.

Dreaming must have inspectable base and project instructions with revision history, manual and scheduled triggers, budgets, cancellation, and bounded execution. Every run must record the instruction revisions, source scope, usage, actual outcome, and errors or unfinished work.

Dreaming must verify against current evidence, preserve provenance and human corrections, and separate direct permitted changes from proposals requiring review. Dispatch success must not be reported as successful consolidation. Partial and budget-exhausted runs must remain distinguishable from completed runs.

Direct changes must have an action journal with before and after revisions and a guarded revert path. A revert must not overwrite subsequent human or agent edits; conflicts must be reported and proposals must remain separately identifiable.

Dreaming must automatically apply consolidations when there is no conflict, without requesting approval for each change. Preserve the visibility and project-scoping requirements. Conflicts an automated agent cannot resolve must enter the review queue and notify the user; independent non-conflicting consolidation can continue.

The app must provide an approval or review queue for conflicts an automated agent cannot resolve. Items must show the competing records or proposed change, evidence, origin, affected project and work, and the decision required from the user.

The queue must distinguish a human-escalated decision from a proposal that an authorized agent can review. Agents must not impersonate a human resolution. Resolution must retain actor, rationale, revisions, and resulting changes, with expected-version checks against the records being resolved.

An escalation must pause only the task needing user input and work dependent on that task or merge. Agents must continue unblocked tasks in the feature. The entire feature should wait only when that merge blocks the remaining feature work. Resolving one item must not clear unrelated conflicts; existing instructions remain effective while a proposal is pending.

In-app notifications must surface required input and other meaningful work events, with direct links to their project, feature, session, review, or report. Notifications must be available from the main chat and detailed workspaces.

The global inbox must support read and unread state, category filtering, and duplicate suppression. Reading or dismissing a notification must not resolve its linked review item. Resolution and acknowledgment are separate operations.

Notification policy should cover decisions, failures, blocked work, significant completions, review changes, budget or authentication problems, and dreaming reports. Feature and issue completion presentation follows confirmed NOTIFY-05. Severity, quiet preferences, aggregation and OS alerts for other categories remain open; required-input OS alerts follow NOTIFY-04.

When the app is not focused, items needing user input must also trigger native operating-system notifications where supported and permitted. Respect OS authorization and notification suppression. Keep the in-app notification and approval item available if OS alerts are denied, unavailable or suppressed. Displaying, reading or dismissing an OS notification must not resolve the decision. Native integration and per-platform behavior require validation.

Verified feature and issue completions must produce highly visible in-app cards floating at the top center below the global toolbar on Chat and every other page. Cards must not reserve layout space, shift content, steal focus or obstruct essential controls. Stack new messages like playing cards, newest first, with access to expand and inspect every message. Keep each card until the user explicitly dismisses it, including across navigation and restart; opening or reading linked work must not dismiss it. Dismissal removes only that card from the stack and retains the notification in history. Provide direct links to completed work, avoid duplicate completion events, and preserve keyboard access, accessible status announcements and reduced-motion behavior. Dismissal or acknowledgment must not resolve approvals or resume work.

title: 17 Platform quality privacy and operations
blocks: Minimum OS targets are macOS 26.2 and Windows 10. Linux is also required, with supported distributions and versions to be determined during architecture validation from what the chosen components can support. Do not claim every Linux distribution is supported. Core installation and launch must not require preinstalled .NET, Node or Python. The same primary Rust codebase must provide the selected behavior; CPU architectures, packaging formats and the validated compatibility matrix remain to specify.

The application must work without an app server or separately administered storage infrastructure. Local browsing, planning edits, and history inspection must remain useful without provider connectivity. Provider-dependent actions must show their actual waiting or failure state.

Dependency claims must distinguish the app runtime from optional semantic helpers, Git, repository build toolchains, and optional local inference. The app must detect missing tools and state exactly which operation needs them; optional components must not become accidental startup requirements.

The app must feel fast, modern, and lightweight. Startup, idle memory and CPU, installed size, active indexing, graph queries, transcript scrolling, and multiple concurrent agents must be measured separately rather than summarized by a single unverified footprint claim.

UI lists and transcripts must scale through incremental updates and bounded rendering. Indexing, vector caches, process output retention, provider concurrency, and background schedules must have visible resource controls. Numeric targets and benchmark datasets remain open.

Use one normal desktop user context. Store secrets through appropriate OS facilities, redact them from ordinary logs, and show what project content is sent to external providers. A separate local web login and OS user switching must not be part of ordinary use.

Autonomous filesystem, shell, network, Git, and integration access must be governed by explicit project scope and user policy, with attribution and interruptibility. A Git worktree provides write isolation, not a security sandbox. Any stronger optional isolation must not recreate mandatory VM infrastructure.

Make agent access and trust restrictions configurable, supporting broad/full-access use as well as users who prefer tighter restrictions. Full access is the initial default for new projects; tighter access remains selectable. Show effective permissions and access mode in Settings. Existing role restrictions, including always-read-only code reviewers, explicit approvals and the prohibition on force-pushing main remain effective; full access does not waive them. Configuration scope and OS-enforced isolation options require architecture validation without mandatory VM infrastructure.

Provide basic safety checks on tool calls to prevent accidental deletion of entire drives or repositories. Keep these checks active even for full-access agents. Check destructive operations before dispatch, expose blocked operations and their rationale, and preserve attribution in the relevant work history. These are additional guards, not replacements for configured tool permissions. Drive/filesystem roots remain blocked. Deliberate deletion of a registered primary repository requires a dedicated user-confirmed action; agents cannot bypass this with operation approval or full access.

Centralize safety preflight for built-in and brokered shell/process, MCP and package tool calls. Resolve actual deletion targets, including path roots, parent traversal, wildcards and links/reparse points; protect filesystem/volume roots and registered repository roots. Avoid relying only on literal command-name or string matching. Distinguish bounded cleanup of owned task worktrees from deletion of a primary repository. Define enforcement for opaque tools and native executable add-ons honestly: harness policy checks alone do not provide OS confinement against arbitrary code running with the user’s permissions. Validate any stronger claimed restriction at the process/OS boundary. Rule coverage, bypass resistance and platform-specific enforcement remain architecture validation work.

The app must provide local diagnostics for storage, queue health, orphan processes, indexing, provider failures, and recovery. Data export, backup/restore, schema migration, and update behavior must preserve authored records and explain failures.

The app must not require a central product account or remote control plane for normal operation. Repository hosting and provider integrations may use their own credentials. Provider connections follow ROUTE-09–10; Git-host authentication methods still need selection and documentation.

Provide first-class agent tools for testing websites through browser control and for testing native desktop applications through computer control. UI tests must exercise the application under development and expose their activity and results in the harness. Browser control does not change the native egui UI decision.

Use browser DOM/accessibility targets and native accessibility controls where available, with screenshots and pointer/keyboard input when needed. Native automation needs platform adapters and explicit permission/capability status on macOS, Windows and Linux. Unsupported controls or missing permissions must produce visible limitations rather than false test success.

Link UI test sessions, actions, screenshots, assertions, failures and relevant browser/process logs to the feature, task, responsible agent and tested repository revision. The user must be able to inspect, interrupt and redirect testing. Record observed outcomes; completing an input action alone does not prove a workflow passed.

Isolate concurrent browser sessions and test data. Coordinate access to shared desktop focus, mouse and keyboard through the resource reservation system under RES-01–03 so agents cannot interfere with each other. This resource constraint must not become a global subagent-count cap. If the user is active, desktop takeover requires OK or Wait under UIQA-05; idle detection and approval lifetime remain open. Mutating UI tests must run under an authorized testing/implementation role, preserving always-read-only reviewers.

Before taking control of a desktop that is not idle, ask the user and offer OK or Wait. OK authorizes the pending takeover; Wait defers it and must not be treated as approval. Do not inject input or steal focus while awaiting the answer or after Wait. Show the request and waiting state in the app. Independent feature work must continue. Idle detection and retry mechanics remain to be specified.

Provide a resource reservation system modeled on CodeGraph resources and holds, exposed through first-class tools and visible in the UI. Support named resources with capacity, acquire, renew and release operations, resource/holder/waiter inspection, purpose, priority, expiry and ownership linked to the feature, task and agent session. Reservations coordinate finite resources such as desktop input, test environments, ports, databases and constrained hardware; they are distinct from per-feature and per-issue subagent limits.

Use a canonical resource identity across projects for physically shared resources, including one machine desktop. Scope project-private resources separately. Enforce ownership and capacity at harness-controlled operation dispatch for resources such as desktop input; CodeGraph advisory holds alone are insufficient to prevent concurrent input. Queue unavailable resources by priority and FIFO within a priority; unrelated tasks continue.

Persist reservation state and use atomic allocation, idempotent retries and explicit renewal. Track grant, release, expiry, cancellation, queue position and unreachable ownership. An expired lease does not prove its process stopped: stop or reconcile old writers and reject stale owners before transferring a physical resource. Show recovery and reservation history in the UI, including pause, shutdown and sleep/wake reconciliation.

Backend selection remains open. Playwright is a browser-automation candidate, not a chosen dependency; browser binaries and any driver/helper runtime need a provisioning plan consistent with the Rust rewrite and no preinstalled Node/Python/.NET requirement. Framework test harnesses can complement full desktop testing; egui_kittest offers Rust UI interactions and snapshots for the harness itself and compatible egui targets. Native computer control is still needed for broader application and OS integration testing.

egui is selected based on the user’s positive experience with the artcraft projects. Implementation must still validate long streaming transcripts, rich text and code, large boards, graph and schema exploration, editable settings, accessible controls, diff rendering, pane resizing, clipboard, shortcuts, and packaging on the three platforms. Those checks validate the selected toolkit rather than reopen its selection.

Provide an application update function using GitHub Releases from the repository where this application will be hosted. While the app is open, automatically poll that repository every hour for a newer release. The product repository is SceneWorks/DevWorks at https://github.com/SceneWorks/DevWorks; use its GitHub Releases for update discovery. Update checking must not require a separate application server or a background harness process after exit.

Always display the currently installed application version in the lower-left sidebar. When a newer release is available to download, indicate its availability in that same lower-left area and provide access to the download/update action. Continue showing the installed version while an update is available or downloaded; only an applied update changes that displayed current version.

Distinguish update checking, available, downloading, staged, applying and failed states. Resolve the correct OS/CPU release asset, validate version and artifact integrity, show progress and retry/cancel where applicable, and preserve the working installed version on failed download or preparation. Update the bundled local Help with the corresponding app version. Preserve work/state and existing shutdown/manual-resume rules during installation/restart; self-improvement activation still requires explicit approval under SELF-03. Automatic background download and approval before installation/restart are confirmed under UPDATE-04. The architecture adopts stable releases by default with explicit prerelease opt-in, due launch/hourly checks, signed staging and approved installation/restart. Native offline/rate-limit, signature and platform installation/rollback qualification remains required.

Automatically download newly available application updates in the background. Require explicit user approval before installing the update and restarting the app. Release discovery or a completed download must not count as that approval. While approval is pending or declined, retain the running installed version and allow existing authorized work to continue. Apply approved updates with the existing work-preservation, shutdown and selective-resume rules; include the matching local Help version.

title: 18 Settings integrations and tool access
intro: Settings becomes a full navigable workspace rather than a small modal. It must make a broad configuration surface manageable without occupying the main chat during ordinary work.
blocks: Codex, Claude, OpenRouter and generic OpenAI-compatible endpoints; provider sign-in/keys, catalogs, routing policies, optional per-feature spending limits with warnings at 75%, supported prompt-cache controls and diagnostics. Usage/cost and cache-efficiency reporting remain separate.
Outgoing servers and tool selection; incoming DevWorks server enablement, stdio/HTTP setup, per-client project/worktree scopes, read selection, explicit command grants, revocation and diagnostics.

One GitHub.com account, personal and organization repositories, authorization, repository associations, PR/check/review access, inbound issue updates, paced automatic triage and verified-resolution publication, polling status and integration diagnostics.
App-level and project-level inference tasks with saved instructions/actions, plus maintenance jobs; schedules, targets, enabled state, run history, triggers, concurrency and failure policy.
Manual discovery, indexing, schema synchronization, selected analysis, graph maintenance, and other retained operations.
Connections/file paths, schema indexing scope, freshness and errors; separate configurable read/write access for agent data tools. These target databases are distinct from app storage.
Inspect and edit instructions for workspace coordinators, feature coordinators, workers, reviewers and dreaming agents.
Shared built-in/MCP selection, effective access for every agent, mandatory read-only reviewer restriction, and availability diagnostics.
Shared skills in ~/.agents/skills and a dedicated harness skills directory; creation, management, scope, activation, version, provenance, and agent applicability.
Choose an app-wide default and project overrides for Docker, Podman or Apple container on supported Macs; inspect installation, engine availability, configuration, capabilities and diagnostics.
Browser and desktop testing capabilities, backend/runtime availability, OS permissions, target selection, resource reservations, diagnostics and desktop-sharing policy.
Language packs and harness packages; install/update/enable/disable/uninstall, configuration, versions, project scope, contributions, approval proposals, access, prerequisites and diagnostics.

Notifications, keep-computer-awake option, resource and per-feature/per-issue subagent limits, artifact storage and retention, backup, appearance, and local diagnostic controls. Configure the app-wide local-repository base directory and optional project overrides. Configure optional per-project keep-working mode; expose its effective state and activity in the project.

Configure broad/full or restricted agent access; show effective permissions and destructive-operation guards. Full access retains reviewer restrictions, approval rules and whole-drive/repository deletion checks.
Settings must expand into a substantial categorized screen covering the required topics. It must remain accessible from the existing navigation while keeping chat as the opening interface.

Settings must provide discoverable categories and search, show configuration scope and effective values, validate edits, preserve unsaved changes, and distinguish configured values from connection health or runtime availability. Exact subnavigation and placement remain design decisions.

Settings must let the user inspect, edit and save instructions for every agent role, including workspace coordinator, feature coordinator, worker, code reviewer and dreaming. Edited instructions must remain subject to harness-enforced policies, including mandatory read-only reviewers; prompt edits cannot grant tools or override those policies. Active agents adopt edits at their next safe step under SET-04; repository instructions take precedence over default roles under user directions and enforced permissions.

Running agents must adopt user-saved or approved edits to their role instructions at their next safe step, without requiring a new session or manual restart. Unapproved agent proposals must not take effect. Retain the instructions used for completed work and preserve effective tool restrictions, user directions and unresolved blockers.

Agents may draft changes to their role instructions, but explicit user approval is required before applying or activating those changes. Preserve version history and provide rollback. Approved changes reach active agents at their next safe step under SET-04; pending or rejected proposals leave the current instructions effective. Approval does not override user directions or configured tool permissions.

Stage agent-authored skill and role-instruction proposals separately from active files, using the approval queue and notifications. Show the affected scope, file changes, rationale, agent/work provenance and validation. Bind approval to the reviewed revision; changed proposals or concurrent user edits require reconciliation. Record approval/rejection and application outcomes. Apply only approved changes, retain prior versions, and keep unrelated authorized work running while approval is pending.

Provide an app-wide preferred base directory for local repositories in Settings, with an optional override per project. Projects without an override inherit the app-wide default. Users must be able to choose their preferred repository location rather than rely on a fixed application path.

Provide a directory chooser and editable path, persist the repository base directory and report invalid or unavailable locations. Use it as the default destination for new repository clones while retaining support for repositories located elsewhere. Changing the setting must not move existing repositories or alter their recorded paths. Keep this setting distinct from harness artifact storage and worktree placement. Show the effective directory and whether it is inherited or overridden. Default path and clone-destination naming remain open.

Provide an app-wide preferred container-system setting with optional per-project overrides, supporting Docker and Podman for projects that require containers. Projects without an override inherit the app-wide backend; clearing an override restores inheritance. Harness tools must honor the selected backend for container operations rather than require Docker for all projects. Container runtimes are optional project dependencies, not prerequisites for starting or using the harness itself.

Offer Apple’s first-party container tooling as an additional backend on supported Macs where feasible. Detect supported OS/CPU and installed tooling and clearly show unavailable or unsupported states. Do not describe it as a universally preinstalled macOS capability. Rust host code may integrate with the optional external tool; no Swift development toolchain is required merely by choosing this backend. Validate the supported operation set before claiming parity with Docker or Podman.

Use backend adapters for image build/pull, container create/start/stop, command execution, inspection and logs, reporting supported operations explicitly. Show selected versus effective backend, executable/connection, version, health and errors in Settings. Record project/work/agent attribution, coordinate shared ports and other resources, and enforce existing tool permissions and read-only reviewer restrictions. Require normal system-install approval for installing runtimes. Do not silently substitute another backend or assume OCI-image compatibility guarantees Compose, networking, volume or Docker API compatibility. Closing the app stops agent-work containers under CONTAINER-04. Initial backend default, multi-service support, ownership/recovery mechanics and container lifecycle across pause, archive and deletion remain open.

When the app closes, stop containers launched for agent work. Leave pre-existing and manually managed containers running. Preserve attribution so shutdown targets the agent-work containers rather than stopping the selected engine or all of its containers. Stopping is not permission to delete containers, images, volumes or stored data. Exact ownership detection, stop failure/recovery and restart behavior remain to specify.

Container reference checked 1 November 2026: Apple container requires a separate signed installer and Apple silicon; its current README supports macOS 26. It runs OCI Linux images in lightweight VMs: https://github.com/apple/container . Podman uses managed VMs on macOS/Windows: https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-machine.1.html . Podman Compose invokes an external provider: https://docs.podman.io/en/latest/markdown/podman-compose.1.html . Exact release/platform capability compatibility must be verified during implementation.

Settings must provide a keep-awake option, off by default, on macOS, Windows and Linux. While enabled and the app is open, prevent idle system sleep even without active work, but allow the display to turn off. Closing the app ends its keep-awake request.

Use the operating system power-management facility to request prevention of idle system sleep. Show the configured value and whether the request is effective or unavailable; disabling the option releases the request. Do not imply that it prevents explicit sleep, lid-close behavior, shutdown, or every OS power policy. The setting defaults to off and allows display sleep under POWER-01.

Support both MCP directions: connect to external MCP servers alongside first-class built-in tools, and expose a DevWorks MCP server for other clients and harnesses. Users manage external server configurations and select the capabilities available to DevWorks agents. The earlier client-only decision is superseded.

The supported transport and capability matrix must be explicit. Configure app-launched local processes and remote server connections where supported, with executable/arguments or endpoint, environment, working directory, authentication references, connection testing, start/stop or reconnect, capability discovery, and failure diagnostics.

MCP tools must retain server identity and schemas, avoid name collisions, follow the same access policy and attribution rules as built-in tools, and link invocation inputs, results, failures, timeouts, and external effects to the responsible agent session and work.

External servers may need optional runtimes such as Node or Python. The app must show those dependencies and failures explicitly without making them prerequisites for launching or using core functionality. Missing or unhealthy servers must not stall unrelated work.

Tool discovery, server capability changes, resources and prompts where supported, and any server-initiated inference requests need an explicit compatibility and authority policy. Inference initiated through this integration must still follow the application router. This requirement governs outgoing client integration; incoming clients use the DevWorks server boundary under MCP-07–11.

When an MCP server is added, enable its read-only tools by default. Users must be able to choose which tools are available through individual toggles and an easy Select all control. Automatic enablement applies to read-only tools; other tools become available through user selection. Show the effective selection in Settings.

Other MCP-compatible clients and harnesses must be able to use DevWorks indexed code, planned work and Knowledge. Preserve code search, architecture/dependency/source retrieval, plans/features/issues/tasks and their histories, and Knowledge claims/evidence/conventions/document retrieval with the same scope, freshness and provenance as first-class application tools.

Provide native stdio and Streamable HTTP access through a server adapter to the shared application gateway. Stdio uses a small installed bridge to the running desktop app; HTTP is opt-in and loopback-bound. Closing the app makes the server unavailable and must not leave a daemon or a second store writer. Publish version-qualified setup instructions and an explicit protocol/capability compatibility matrix.

Incoming clients require individually authorized, revocable identities and explicit project/repository/worktree scopes. Default grants allow selected reads only. Human configuration controls connection approval, credential provisioning, tool/resource visibility and any write grants. Check current authority before invocation and publication; protocol metadata, client labels, tool annotations and resource URIs cannot grant authority. Credentials and private application/package transports are never exposed.

Allow explicitly selected work and Knowledge mutations through existing typed commands, revisions, approvals, attribution, idempotency receipts and recovery rules. An external harness cannot impersonate a human, self-grant permissions, bypass reviewer restrictions or clear human-only execution holds. Index refresh or inference is an explicit separately granted command, never a hidden effect of context retrieval. Keep external inference and provider credentials owned by the external harness unless it explicitly invokes an authorized DevWorks operation.

Expose discoverable tools and scoped resources, with optional context prompts, bounded pagination/results and precise unsupported or unavailable outcomes. Preserve view/source identity, citations, coverage gaps and work revisions; support cancellation and durable status/receipt recovery after disconnection without duplicate effects. Qualify at least two independent clients across both transports, including revoked scopes, isolated overlays, denied writes and restart behavior before advertising compatibility.

The app must provide GitHub configuration and integration as a supported product capability, with visible account/host configuration, repository associations, authorization status, and access to linked PRs, checks, and code reviews.

GitHub credentials, token scopes and failures must be inspectable without exposing secrets. Git transport credentials and GitHub API authorization must be distinguished. Use the single GitHub.com account and organization support under GH-03. Use direct API polling under GH-10. Authentication method and additional Git hosts remain open; multiple-account and Enterprise support are not required by the agreed scope.

Support one GitHub.com account, including personal repositories and repositories owned by organizations the account can access. Organization-owned repositories must support discovery, project association and the same authorized PR, check, review and delivery workflows as personal repositories. Preserve repository owner identity and respect actual account and repository permissions; organization support must not require signing in as another user.

Always display references to GitHub resources as clickable links to the corresponding resource. Apply this across coordinator/agent messages, task and feature details, source-control views, activity/history, reviews, notifications and other app surfaces. This includes repositories, branches, commits, issues, PRs, reviews and checks/workflow runs when referenced. Use identifiable labels with repository/owner context where needed; a bare resource number, name or hash must not substitute for the link.

For linked GitHub issues, automatically reflect remote updates in local tracking. Keep intermediate execution details local. Once work is completed and verified, automatically post a resolution summary and close the GitHub issue. Verify and use clarification about the same bug; genuinely new scope or feature requests require a user decision. Remote closure does not stop a verified bug already being fixed or approved/planned feature work. Close the local copy of an unstarted unreproducible bug; retain feature requests for manual decision. Preserve identity and source links; locally created issues stay local until explicitly published/linked.

Persist remote identity, observations, routed local work, import checkpoints and publication receipts. Deduplicate import/triage, coalesce updates and separate remote fields from local workflow, plan, pauses, budgets and private history. Use durable paced intake and outbox effects with echo suppression, bounded retries and observation-first recovery. Resolution publication binds verified completion/integration evidence; uncertain comment/close outcomes are reconciled before retry. Show queued/running/failed/conflicted state and authentication/rate-limit failures. Reopening a remote issue cannot clear a human pause or authorize resumed work.

Agents verify and incorporate GitHub clarification about the same bug. Genuinely new scope or feature requests are held for a user decision with an in-app notification. Agents reconcile other conflicting updates automatically, retaining both versions, provenance and rationale. If unresolved, preserve both versions and escalate through the approval queue with an in-app notification. Only conflicting changes and affected work wait; unrelated work continues. Reconciliation cannot override user directions, permissions or pauses, or publish intermediate local execution details.

Locally created issues stay local until explicitly published to GitHub or linked to an existing GitHub issue. Creation/editing never implicitly publishes or links them. After explicit linking/publication, apply inbound updates and verified-resolution publication under GH-05; retain local identity/history and configured permissions. Do not mirror every local edit or workflow status to GitHub.

Automatically import existing open GitHub issues when connecting a repository and every newly reported issue thereafter. Queue automatic agent triage app-wide, admitting at most one issue every 30 minutes by default, with the interval configurable in Settings. Keep waiting issues visible without starting agents or catch-up bursts. Triage bug reports versus feature requests, verify reported bugs and immediately start verifiable bugs under existing execution controls. Notify in-app for feature requests or unverifiable bugs. Shared repositories have no single issue-owning project: triage routes incoming reports to relevant project context. Projects retain their own issues/features; feature coordinators and the message board coordinate overlapping work.

Use direct GitHub API polling from the Rust application to discover relevant repository, push, PR/merge, issue, review and check/workflow changes. Use authenticated conditional requests where supported, respecting GitHub rate limits, retry guidance and endpoint poll-interval headers. No webhook receiver, public endpoint, tunnel or relay is required. Poll while the app is open and reconcile remote state after reopening, sleep/wake or connectivity recovery. Remote-state reconciliation must not replay missed scheduled inference runs or implicitly resume paused work.

Changes discovered by GitHub polling must produce application events used both to notify relevant agents/coordinators and to trigger appropriate repository indexing updates. Events must retain their source repository and relevant work/PR context so notifications and index changes can be inspected alongside the affected work. Code-affecting changes such as pushes and merges must cause the affected indexed code to be refreshed; issue/review-only changes must not require a code reindex. Preserve source revision and visible index freshness.

Persist observed GitHub state and deduplicated application events in the existing SQLite runtime, with separate delivery/progress state for agent notification and indexing consumers. Repeated polls/restarts must not duplicate agent notices or indexing side effects. Deliver events to the responsible agent sessions as inspectable external updates without replacing user directions or clearing pauses; show undelivered updates. For code events, reconcile the affected configured ref/revision with remote content before incremental indexing, coalesce redundant pending refreshes and expose queued/running/failed/stale state and logs. An index failure must not suppress the corresponding agent event. Define initial baselines, event ordering, polling cadence, indexed-ref scope and replay/recovery mechanics before implementation.

Settings must provide an explicit Auto-Merge on/off control, enabled by default with project and repository overrides. The target autonomous workflow supports committing, pushing, responding to reviews, fixing findings, and merging without routine human intervention. With Auto-Merge off, the workflow must stop before merge while other authorized work may continue.

Mandatory independent code review before merge defaults to on, with project/repository overrides and a separate-agent fix/review cycle. Configured GitHub automated reviews normally satisfy it. Use an independent in-app reviewer when automation is absent, fails or never completes. Automation failure must not indefinitely prevent delivery; fallback still requires complete review and resolution of every actionable finding.

Use configured GitHub review automation normally; automatically fall back to an independent in-app reviewer if it fails or never completes. Avoid duplicate fallback launches. Bind review evidence and findings to the exact current head and source identity, including explicit completion with zero findings. Keep actionable external findings in the fix cycle even if fallback is used. Fallback satisfies the DevWorks review requirement without bypassing required checks, permissions or branch protection. Changed heads need current review evidence; all actionable findings must be resolved before merge.

Auto-Merge and mandatory-review policy must be configurable per repository with inherited defaults from project and workspace settings. Auto-Merge and mandatory independent review both default to on; project settings may override each inherited value, and repository settings may override each project value. The effective value and source of each value, including local overrides, must be visible. One repository’s review setup must not be assumed to apply to every repository in its project.

Every actionable review finding must be resolved before an automatic merge, including minor findings. A severity threshold alone must not permit unresolved actionable findings. The feature coordinator adjudicates disputed or non-actionable findings, recording its rationale in the linked review history. Findings it judges actionable must still be fixed.

Merge readiness must reconcile the current code revision, required checks, the review source selected under DELIVERY-02–03, all actionable findings, effective policy, and cross-repository dependencies. Apply the effective repository review and Auto-Merge policy to both task/group PRs into the feature branch and the final feature PR into main. Review findings, fixes, re-reviews, dismissals and reasons must remain linked to the feature, PR, revision, and participating agents.

The maximum number of fix/review cycles must be configurable in Settings, with a default of 3. Execution must honor the configured limit rather than continue an unbounded fix loop. Reaching the limit does not waive the requirement to resolve every actionable finding before merge.

If the feature coordinator cannot reach a decision, it must raise the issue to the user and publish an in-app notification. This applies to unresolved review disputes or fix-cycle outcomes it cannot resolve. The escalation must retain the relevant findings, attempts, evidence, and coordinator rationale; unresolved actionable findings continue to block that merge. Escalation must not pause independent feature work: only the affected task and its dependent work wait.

Provide separate settings for agent-initiated deployments and release publishing. Each has Automatic, Ask me and Disabled values and defaults to Ask me. Inherit workspace defaults through project settings, with independent per-repository overrides; show effective values and their sources. These controls are independent of each other and of Auto-Merge. Ask me requires explicit user approval before the action; Disabled prevents it; Automatic permits it subject to existing tool permissions and applicable execution rules. A merge is not deployment or release approval. Harness self-improvement installation/restart still requires explicit approval under SELF-03.
Users must be able to manage which tools agents can access, primarily through Settings. Management must cover built-in application tools, tools supplied by MCP servers and package-provided tools.

The effective tool set must be inspectable for an agent/session, derived from the shared selection under TOOL-04 and the mandatory reviewer restriction under TOOL-05. MCP defaults follow MCP-06. Shell/process and web defaults follow TOOL-06 and TOOL-08. Define remaining built-in defaults, denial precedence, and effects on queued and active runs. Disabled tools must be enforced at invocation time rather than merely omitted from prompts.

Record tool policy revisions and changes with actor attribution. Tool descriptions and schemas are not authority to exceed user policy. Preserve explicit user selections during tool discovery. Define how read-only classification is established, how missing or conflicting metadata is handled, and how later tool additions or capability changes affect saved selections. Initial MCP defaults and selection controls follow MCP-06.

The configured tool selection applies to every agent, rather than requiring separate selections for coordinators, coding agents, and reviewers. Code-review agents must have access to the same selected read tools as the other agents.

Code-review agents must always be read-only. The harness must deny write/edit and other mutating operations, including indirect writes through shell/process tools, while preserving the shared selected read tools. Enforce this for built-in, MCP and package-provided invocations, not only in reviewer instructions; Settings and Select all must not override it. The harness retains review findings and history without granting the reviewer general write access. Fixes belong to separately authorized implementation agents.

Enable built-in shell/process tools by default for implementation agents, subject to configured tool permissions and project scope. Users may disable them in Settings. Default enablement must not grant review agents write access or bypass TOOL-05.

Implementation agents may install project dependencies automatically within authorized project/worktree scope. System-wide tool or package installations require user approval before execution. Configured permissions and read-only reviewer restrictions still apply. Record installation actions and approval outcomes in the associated work history.

Provide built-in web search and page-fetching tools, including documentation retrieval, enabled by default. Apply shared tool selection and invocation permissions, including access for read-only review agents. Retain tool activity, source URLs and results in the responsible agent/work history.

The harness must support the experience of asking an agent to build a package for a missing capability, reviewing the result and activating it without rebuilding the main application. Language packs under ADDON-01–04 are one category within the broader harness package system. Pi and Oh My Pi inform the extension design; the product remains a Rust harness with egui.

Provide a general harness package system using managed executables and a Rust SDK, sharing versioned installation and lifecycle infrastructure with language packs. Packages may contribute agent tools, commands, workflow steps and verification gates, event handlers, context retrieval and compaction extensions, skills, prompts and role instructions, and native UI contributions. Provider extensions must register through the router rather than create a separate inference path. Support local package development and independently installable prebuilt packages without recompiling the main app. Building Rust packages locally requires the appropriate development toolchain; installing compatible prebuilt packages does not. Core use must not require a TypeScript/Bun/Node runtime.

Agents must be able to create and test a package project, explain its capabilities and changes, and propose it for activation. Agent-authored new or changed executable packages require explicit user approval before activation, including updates to active packages. Bind approval to the reviewed package version and contents; record rationale, requested capabilities, dependencies, verification evidence and originating agent/work. Pending or rejected proposals leave the active version unchanged. Package development and tests use authorized worktrees and tool permissions; packaged skills and role-instruction changes retain SKILL-07–09 and SET-05–06 approval rules. Approval to activate a package does not grant approval for every action it later requests.

Package UI contributions must use host-defined descriptions of settings pages, forms, tables, reports, panels, actions and status indicators rendered natively by egui. Packages may request host dialogs and notifications through the same application interfaces. Do not require a WebView or exchange egui objects across the executable boundary. Packages can extend the UI within supported contribution points without rebuilding the host; completely new widget types or host extension points may require a host update. Exact schemas and supported component coverage remain to be specified.

Package actions must use the shared application command/query and tool interfaces and retain project scope, tool selection, read-only reviewer restrictions, work ownership, concurrency/resource limits, plan approval and review/delivery gates. All package-requested inference must pass through the internal router. Context and compaction contributions must preserve original transcripts, user directions, required context and the configured compaction threshold; avoid unnecessary cache changes and record context provenance. Extensions may add checks but must not silently remove required gates. Managed executable separation is not an OS security sandbox: host checks govern brokered operations, and restricting arbitrary native file or network access would require OS isolation. Document the executable trust model honestly.

Broaden Settings Add-ons into one management screen for language packs and general harness packages. Show package type, source, version, contributions, scope, requested/effective access, prerequisites, compatibility, health and logs. Provide install, update, configure, enable, disable and uninstall controls and access to approval proposals. Approved new versions reload at the next safe boundary, retaining the prior version for rollback and recording which package version each agent used. Preserve package state and linked activity through restart; visible failures must not stall unrelated authorized work. Exact state migration, rollback compatibility and active-run transition mechanics remain proposed implementation details.

Extend the common manifest and local process protocol with declared contributions, configuration schemas, scoped host calls, event subscriptions and package state access. The host owns registration, validates messages and results, and attributes tools, commands, hooks, state and UI actions to package/version, agent/session and applicable work. Separate notifications from bounded decision or transformation hooks; define ordering, timeouts, errors and recovery so a failed extension cannot leave a required decision looking successful. Persist subscription progress and action identities where replay is supported to prevent duplicate external effects. Apply package-version changes at explicit safe boundaries and reconcile state before rollback. Protocol details, distribution/trust, dependency resolution, SDK APIs and native UI schemas remain open.
Inspect a proprietary format or gather a release-readiness report.
Run an additional migration check or respond to an indexing failure.
Retrieve domain knowledge or bundle approved skills and role instructions.
Display migration findings in a feature panel with a settings form.
Run a compiler-backed semantic indexer through the language-pack interface.

Reference boundary. Pi bundles TypeScript extensions, skills, prompts and themes. Oh My Pi also uses TypeScript/Bun for its agent runtime and extension loader, alongside substantial Rust native tooling; it is not an all-Rust harness or an existing Rust plugin host. Their extension patterns are design references, and implementation quality or reuse suitability has not been evaluated. Existing Pi/Oh My Pi packages are not automatically compatible with this executable protocol. Direct compatibility would require a separately specified runtime and host-API/UI mappings and is not an agreed implementation requirement.
