Theme contributions can use future host-supported schemas; arbitrary terminal UI components do not automatically become egui components.

Independent tool calls must keep running when another call fails or requires approval, unless that failure makes their execution unsafe or invalid. Hold or cancel only affected calls and their actual dependents. Preserve completed results and reconcile uncertain effects before retry. Existing parent pauses and tool permissions remain effective.

After the user explicitly trusts a publisher for package updates, allow compatible signed updates to activate automatically at a safe boundary provided access does not expand beyond the approved scope. Expanded access requires fresh approval. New or changed agent-authored executable contents still require explicit approval of the exact version and contents under EXT-02, even if signed by a trusted publisher. Preserve active work, prior outcomes and rollback/state compatibility; publisher trust does not authorize future actions outside normal tool, role, work and permission controls.

title: 19 Graph schema health and review workspaces
intro: Code intelligence must have human-facing exploration and management surfaces, not only agent tools. The existing CodeGraph repository home and its navigation are the accepted reference for repository exploration, implemented natively with egui. Database schema navigation and any additional graph-specific views still require detail.
blocks: The app must provide a way to navigate code graphs and their relationships, move between entities and their source context, and inspect graph information within repository and project scope.

Follow the existing CodeGraph repository home and navigation as the baseline for repository exploration. Opening a repository leads to its Overview, with Nodes, Health, and Reviews available directly. Preserve repository identity and indexed revision/freshness, summary and confidence, health and activity indicators, internal code-project analysis, inbound/outbound dependencies, node-type counts and drill-down, and README where available. The workspace coordinator chat remains the application opening screen.

Preserve the CodeGraph drill-down from a repository or internal code project into a node list, optionally filtered by node type, with grouped node kinds, expandable containers and members, and links to node details. Node details retain qualified name, properties, trust/confidence, source location and line-numbered source, and incoming/outgoing relationships grouped by type. Related nodes and cross-repository relationships must be navigable, with breadcrumbs back to repository and node-type context.

Adapt the accepted navigation flow to egui and the multi-repository project model without copying Angular routing or web hosting. Internal code projects/modules must be distinguished from top-level work projects that group repositories. Preserve repository context across home, list and detail views; provide return navigation to the originating workspace. Extra graph visualization controls and saved views remain open rather than replacing the accepted repository home.

Database indexing must be supported alongside repository indexing. The app must manage database indexing sources and connections, including a file path for SQLite or another supported file-backed database.

A database source must declare engine/adapter, display identity, project associations and effective access, file path or connection endpoint, credential references where needed, enabled state, schema selection, and indexing status. Reuse one connection definition across project associations under DB-09. Creating, editing, testing, disabling, reindexing, and removing indexed metadata must be available without deleting or modifying the source database.

Schema indexing must use read-only source access and extract supported tables, columns, types, keys, indexes, views, procedures and relationships. Report coverage per adapter. Indexing does not read row contents into a searchable data index. Agent queries and data mutations are separate operations under DB-04–05.

Database indexing covers schemas only and remains read-only. Separately provide agent tools to read and manipulate data. Each database connection defaults to read-only; data writes require explicit user enablement for that connection. Enforce connection policy together with configured tool permissions and project scope. Enabling writes on one connection must not enable them on others. Code-review agents remain read-only even when connection writes are enabled.

Expose database data tools against configured target connections, with visible effective read/write permissions and project scope. Support queries and permitted data inserts, updates and deletes, with adapter-specific capability reporting, execution/result limits, cancellation and attributed history. Enforce read-only access at the execution/connection boundary where supported, including indirect mutations; SQL keyword checks alone are insufficient. Under DB-08, link schema changes to their migration commit or direct operation, recording the fallback reason and outcome. Define transaction, failure/retry and sensitive-result handling without importing row data into the schema index.

Support SQLite, MariaDB/MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server as target database families for schema indexing and separately permissioned data tools. MariaDB and MySQL must both be covered and verified, with differences reported. These are target connections, independent of the selected SQLite and sqlite-vec internal app storage. Supported engine versions, authentication modes and metadata coverage remain to be qualified. HelixDB and HydraDB are excluded from target readers.

Do not implement a HelixDB schema reader or structural-inference adapter. The user removed this conditional capability on 2 November 2026. Retain historical storage evaluations only as evidence; they neither enable HelixDB connections nor add an internal storage dependency. Schema indexing for the selected relational targets remains metadata-only, with separately permissioned data tools governed by DB-04–06.

Agents may change database schemas, including supported CREATE, ALTER and DROP operations. Prefer migration files committed to the appropriate project repository through its normal worktree, review and delivery workflow. If committed migrations are not possible, direct schema changes are allowed. Applying either route requires writes to be explicitly enabled for the target connection and the agent to have the necessary tool permissions and project scope. A migration commit alone does not authorize application to a database. Indexing and code-review agents remain read-only. Preserve the associated task, agent and action history.

Database connections may be shared across multiple projects, with access controlled per project. Sharing a connection must not automatically grant access to other projects or their agents. Resolve the requesting project and enforce its access together with the connection settings and agent tool permissions on every operation. Project access cannot enable writes while the connection remains read-only. Indexing and code-review agents remain read-only even where project and connection settings permit writes. Retain project and responsible-agent attribution for operations against shared connections.

Users must be able to navigate indexed schemas, inspect their objects and relationships, and understand their connection to code or project work. File-backed database sources must not require an application storage server.

Schema exploration should support object search, table/column details, keys and constraints, relationship traversal, source identity, sync freshness and failures, and code-to-schema references where evidence supports them. Unsupported metadata must not appear as confirmed absent.

Repository health analysis must be visible in the UI, with access to analysis results and the findings that need attention. This is distinct from the health of the app, its stores, or its background workers.

Health results must identify repository/revision, analysis time, coverage, categories and severity where supported, evidence, trends where available, and linked corrective work. Missing, stale, partial, or failed analysis must be distinguished from a healthy result. Scoring and remediation automation remain open.
Code reviews must have a visible management and inspection surface, linked to repositories, features, source changes, PRs, and the agents or users who produced and addressed the findings.

Review views must distinguish local agent reviews from GitHub reviews, support findings and their status, severity, source/diff locations, responses and revisions, and show whether findings remain applicable to the current code. Knowledge conflict approvals must not be mixed into code review state.

title: 20 Conventions and skills
intro: Conventions and skills are required managed inputs to agent behavior. Conventions express reusable guidance and expectations; skills package instructions or procedures for a task. Harness self-improvement is an explicit product goal, including agent-proposed improvements to reusable harness-specific skills and role instructions, applied with user approval. Boundaries with lessons and role instructions must remain explicit.
blocks: Users must be able to manage conventions. The app need not reproduce the CodeGraph wiki interface; a dedicated searchable conventions manager is sufficient if it preserves the required behavior.

Conventions must support creation and editing, search, scope and applicability, activation or retirement, versions, source provenance, and agent retrieval. Project-specific conventions remain scoped to their project under KNOW-07. A session must be able to identify the convention revisions it received. Storage/import format and synchronization with existing sources remain open.

The harness must support skills and provide a way to manage them. Skills must be discoverable to the relevant coordinators and workers rather than existing only as hidden files or duplicated prompt text.

Skill management should support discovery/import, inspection, creation/editing of local skills, enable/disable, scope, version/source identity, and validation of referenced instructions and assets. Skills are file-backed in the shared and harness-specific directories under SKILL-04. Harness-specific skills take precedence over shared skills with the same name. Referenced documents, scripts and assets are supported under SKILL-06. Refine format compatibility, reference resolution, dependency detection and helper invocation mechanics.

A session must record selected skills and their revisions. Skills must obey tool access and user authority, preserve references to lessons they address, and make conflicts with conventions, rules, or role instructions visible. Record skill-version transitions in session history. Apply changes only after in-flight work reaches a safe boundary; do not retroactively rewrite the instructions or evidence for completed steps.

Support using existing shared skill folders from ~/.agents/skills and a separate harness-specific skills directory. Users must be able to create harness-specific skills in that dedicated directory and manage skills from both locations in the app. Shared skills must be usable from their existing location rather than requiring an import copy. Show each skill’s origin, filesystem location, and which version is active. Harness-specific skills take precedence over shared skills with the same name. The exact harness-specific directory path remains open.

When a skill edit is user-saved or approved, running agents using that skill must adopt the updated version at their next safe step, without requiring a new session or manual restart. Unapproved agent proposals must not take effect. Existing tool-access policy, explicit user instructions, and unresolved blockers remain effective.

Support skills containing referenced documents, executable scripts and assets alongside their instructions, in both shared and harness-specific skill directories. Agents must be able to access these resources and invoke permitted scripts. Scripts use normal harness tool permissions and dependency rules; a skill must not grant additional authority or bypass disabled tools, reviewer read-only restrictions, project scope or approval for system-wide installation. Optional skill runtime requirements must remain explicit and must not become prerequisites for core app use.

Agents may draft new harness-specific skills and edits to their own skills, supporting harness self-improvement. Explicit user approval is required before creating or updating the active skill or making the proposed version available to agents. Record the responsible agent, work/session, rationale, revisions and approval outcome in visible history. Existing tool permissions, user directions, dependency rules and next-safe-step adoption still apply. This supersedes the earlier policy allowing automatic skill edits without approval. Agent improvements to shared skills use approved harness-specific overrides under SKILL-09. Harness-code improvements follow SELF-01.

Preserve prior skill versions and show changes, rationale and supporting evidence in the skill manager and linked work history. Provide revision-aware rollback without overwriting later edits silently. Record validation performed and its outcome; an agent’s claim that a skill is improved must not be represented as demonstrated effectiveness. Validation follows EVAL-05 and post-adoption monitoring and rollback proposals follow EVAL-07, preserving the required user approval for agent-authored skill changes under SKILL-07.

For an agent-proposed improvement to a shared skill in ~/.agents/skills, propose a harness-specific override and leave the shared original and its files untouched. User approval is required before creating/updating the active override under SKILL-07. Pending or rejected proposals do not change the effective skill. Once approved, the harness-specific skill takes precedence over its same-name shared source, with active agents adopting it at the next safe step. Preserve source/override provenance and version history.

The harness must be able to propose improvements to its own Rust code and handle them through the normal project feature, PR and review workflow. Use the same planning and approval rules, isolated worktrees, implementation, verification, review/fix cycle and configured merge policy as other project work. Retain linked work, agents, transcripts, Git actions, reviews and evidence. Self-improvement does not bypass configured permissions or delivery gates. Installing the resulting build and restarting the app require explicit approval under SELF-03. Self-improvement proposals carry eval evidence under EVAL-05.

Represent the harness repository as ordinary managed project work. Distinguish the running application version from the source revision, tested candidate build and merged code; a successful merge must not imply the running app has updated. Link build artifacts and verification to the self-improvement feature/task. Implement approval-gated installation/restart under SELF-03. Refine restart preparation, checkpoint/resume, compatibility and rollback mechanics, preserving other work and existing shutdown/resume policies.

Installing a self-improvement build and restarting the app to activate it require explicit user approval. A merged PR or passing tests/reviews must not count as that approval. While approval is pending or denied, continue using the installed version; unrelated authorized work may continue. Applying an approved update must preserve existing shutdown and selective-resume rules. Record approval and update outcomes.

Every agent-authored harness self-improvement must include documentation as part of the work. Update the affected local Help, UI/tool behavior descriptions and developer/extension guides or examples to match the change, including changes to harness code, roles, skills and packages as applicable. Include documentation in the plan and acceptance criteria, deliver it with the change, and verify and review its accuracy and completeness. Missing, stale or incomplete required documentation blocks completion and delivery; it must not be deferred as optional follow-up work. Preserve existing approval and activation rules. Shipped documentation must match the installed version under HELP-05.

Evals are graded measurements of harness behavior, collected from real work and from repeatable trials, compared across revisions of what produced the behavior and attached to improvement proposals. They provide the validation and recovery mechanics SKILL-08 requires: an agent’s claim that a change helps is never evidence by itself. Decisions D1–D9 of the 3 November 2026 evaluation review are recorded in the interview record.

The harness must support eval suites that measure the behavior produced by harness skills, role instructions, harness-specific overrides, conventions and lesson rules delivered to sessions, harness code builds, and model or tier routing assigned to roles. A suite is a versioned asset with its own cases, graders, rubrics, fixtures and accepted exceptions, stored separately from the subject it measures, showing its origin, location and active revision as skills do under SKILL-04. Shared, harness-specific and package-contributed suites are supported; a package may contribute suites only for what it contributes.

Completed and stopped work must be graded automatically from durable history without re-running it: coordinator and worker transcripts and tool calls, Git, PR and review records, and the resulting work state. This covers DevWorks’s own coordinator and worker sessions and the attributed command records of external harnesses connected as MCP clients under MCP-10; DevWorks holds no external harness transcripts and does not import them. Attribute graded behavior at the step level to the revisions in effect when it happened (skills, roles, overrides, conventions, rules, routing and running app version). A session can span several revisions under SKILL-05; a result that cannot be attributed to one revision belongs to an explicit mixed-revision group, never silently to one side. Grading reads only and never changes work, repositories, remotes or Knowledge.

Support deterministic checks over the event record, outcome checks over work state, model-graded rubrics through the internal router, and human verdicts. Every grader names the requirement, skill section or rule it enforces, and a check that measures only a proxy, such as a command pattern rather than intent, says so. A model-graded result records the judge model and settings, rubric revision, sampled instances and their population, and each verdict with its reason; each instance receives several independent votes and split votes are reported. A judge verdict is never presented as a deterministic result. A judge configuration is calibrated against human verdicts on a sample before its results can gate approval under EVAL-05, and its agreement rate is shown with its results; changing the judge model, settings or rubric is a measurement change under EVAL-06. All model-based judging, including production grading, is live inference under TEST-03; tests of the eval machinery use scripted judges and fixtures under TEST-02.

Support repeatable trials that run agent work against frozen inputs, such as snapshots of work records and repository revisions, in an isolated workspace. Trials may write only to disposable copies: throwaway repositories and remotes and stateful substitutes for the tracker, GitHub and other external services, so claiming, implementation, review and delivery can be evaluated end to end. Production destinations, real accounts and real credentials are unreachable from a trial; a case may also refuse all writes. Substitute services expose the real services’ tool schemas. Each case runs a configured number of times, and results report each run’s score, the share of runs that passed and whether every run passed. Trials are live inference under TEST-03 and never run within unit or integration tests. Each snapshot records its source, time, content identity and expected answer.

Every change to an evaluable subject under EVAL-01 must carry eval evidence. For changes that need approval, run the applicable trials against the baseline and the candidate before the proposal is presented. For changes that take effect without approval, including user-saved edits, dreaming consolidations under DREAM-05 and user routing changes, record the comparison when it can run and always monitor after adoption under EVAL-07; evaluation adds no approval step where none exists. The comparison shows the target metric’s change and every other metric’s change with its method and uncertainty under EVAL-09, the run count and coverage under EVAL-14. Evidence is labeled improved, regressed, inconclusive or unvalidated. It is unvalidated when no applicable suite exists, the suite could not run or either arm falls below the suite’s minimum sample or coverage; inconclusive is reserved for an adequately measured comparison without a meaningful difference. For an agent-authored change, regressed or unvalidated evidence blocks approval unless the user overrides it with a recorded reason; inconclusive evidence is shown without blocking. The user’s own edits carry evidence without a gate. Eval evidence never replaces approval. Evidence is bound to immutable identities of the candidate and baseline, suite and case revisions, fixtures, grader and judge configurations, accepted exceptions and trial settings. Both arms use the same measurement revisions and settings except the declared subject under test; when that subject is a routing or model assignment, all other settings including the judge stay the same. Approval binds to the evaluated candidate; a later change to the candidate or to a measurement input it depends on returns the proposal to unvalidated until re-evaluated.

A subject under evaluation must not be able to change its own measurement. Agents may draft suites, cases, graders, rubrics and fixtures; activating them requires user approval as a separate proposal with its own history. One proposal must not change both a subject and a suite that measures it. Accepted exceptions are authored by a person and record the check, matched instance, reason and approver.

After a change is adopted, production grading continues and compares the new revision with the previous one under EVAL-09. When a monitored metric regresses past its declared criterion, notify the user with the evidence and propose a rollback; a rollback never happens without user approval. Use the subject’s own activation mechanism: SKILL-08 revision-aware rollback for skills, roles and overrides; the revision and lifecycle mechanisms of CONV-02, KNOW-03 and DREAM-04 for conventions and lesson rules; the settings revision for role routing; and reinstallation of a prior build for app builds, which also requires SELF-03 approval, a compatibility check of stored data and migrations made since that build, and the SELF-02 restart and rollback mechanics. A build whose data changes cannot be safely reversed is reported as not rollback-capable, with the reason. A rollback preserves later unrelated edits or reports the conflict without overwriting them, and is monitored like any other change.

Failing checks must trace to the rule, skill section or lesson they enforce, with links to the exact transcript, tool call or record under HISTORY-01. Recurring failures should become candidate improvements in the Knowledge and dreaming flow with their eval evidence attached, such as a skill or role edit, hook, test or harness-code task, and feed the lesson recurrence views of KNOW-04 and KNOW-05. Before a failure becomes a proposal, sampled failing instances are checked so a grader defect is not reported as agent behavior, and that check and its outcome are recorded.

Results show counts with denominators, runs, coverage and revision groups, never a bare percentage. Each metric declares its comparison method, uncertainty measure and minimum effect; for example, a binary outcome reports the difference in proportions with a confidence interval, and a judged rubric includes the judge calibration. A difference whose uncertainty includes no change, or that falls short of the declared minimum effect, is inconclusive, and improvement is never claimed from a single run or case. Requirements fix no numeric thresholds; suites start with values labeled provisional, which are replaced by measured values and are never acceptance thresholds. Trial comparisons match cases, fixtures, models, tools, budgets and measurement revisions in both arms except the declared subject under test. Production comparisons use common measurement revisions for both cohorts, regrading retained evidence under one revision where available; otherwise the comparison is non-comparable and never triggers a regression notice or rollback proposal. Production comparisons disclose cohort differences in task mix and size, projects, models, routing and other revisions changed in the same period; a change coinciding with another change to the same behavior is reported as confounded. Where possible, validation uses cases other than those that motivated a proposal, and results say which were which.

Trials and model-graded judging run through the internal router with attributed usage and costs under ROUTE-17, linked to the suite run and any proposal they validate. Suites run on demand, automatically when a proposal is created and on a schedule, and show the expected run count and cost estimate before a trial run starts. On-demand and proposal-triggered eval runs support a spending limit that pauses the run when reached. Scheduled eval runs follow JOB-09: they report usage and costs without a spending limit.

Provide a dedicated Evals area showing each suite’s cases and graders, latest results by revision, trends across revisions, failing instances linked to their evidence and accepted exceptions. Each proposal in the approval queue under REVIEW-01 shows its eval comparison and evidence status.

Agents can list suites, read results and evidence, run permitted suites and draft suite changes through the same operations as the UI, under normal tool access, project scope and authority. An agent cannot approve proposals, accept exceptions or activate suite changes without the approval EVAL-06 requires.
Suites are documented under SELF-04: what each measures, what each grader checks and cannot check, how to run it and how to read its results. Suite documentation ships with the suite version.

Every instance, run and suite result has one explicit outcome: passed, failed, unclear, not applicable, evidence unavailable (for example a truncated external transcript or missing record), grader error, cancelled or budget exhausted. Report coverage with every rate: eligible, graded and ungraded instances, with reasons. Only passed and failed outcomes enter pass and fail rates; incomplete evidence never counts as a pass or silently leaves a denominator. Each suite declares per metric the minimum usable sample and required coverage a result needs to count as evidence under EVAL-05.

title: 21 Scheduled tasks operations and indexing diagnostics
intro: Users need to schedule inference tasks at app and project scope, run maintenance jobs and manual operations, and understand failures. All use the app’s durable runtime, router policies and observable history while the desktop application is running.
blocks: The app must manage scheduled background jobs, including the selected CodeGraph job types. Settings must expose schedules and controls, while run status and meaningful outcomes remain visible from related workspaces.

Job records must include type, target/scope, schedule and timezone, enabled state, parameters, last and next run, and linked execution history. Create/edit, pause/enable, Run now, inspect, and supported cancellation/retry controls must be available. Scheduled inference overlap is skipped under JOB-08. Define checkpoint/reconciliation mechanics, failure/backoff, resource controls and usage reporting without job spending limits under JOB-09; missed occurrences are skipped under JOB-03 and interrupted runs resume under JOB-04.

Enabled maintenance and scheduled inference tasks at app/project scope reactivate automatically when the app reopens, independently of manual feature and issue resumption. Missed occurrences stay missed: compute the next future occurrence without replaying them, coalescing them into an immediate catch-up run or launching a startup catch-up batch. Runs already active when the app closed resume under JOB-04.

Maintenance and scheduled inference runs active at app closure resume automatically on reopening, without waiting for their next due time or requiring feature or issue resumption. Continue the interrupted run with its existing identity, progress and history; this does not replay missed occurrences. Preserve separate user pauses, budget holds and approval waits. Job resumption must not implicitly resume feature or issue agents paused by app closure; those require manual Continue.

Support scheduled inference tasks at both project level and app level. Each task must be configurable to run instructions and perform automated actions through the harness’s tools and router. A required use case is periodically checking a GitHub repository for newly reported issues and performing a configured automated action. Project tasks retain their project context; app-level tasks can cover configured work across projects. Scheduled actions remain subject to effective tool permissions and existing approval policies.

Manage each inference schedule’s name, scope/targets, saved prompt, schedule/timezone, enabled state, routing and usage reporting without job spending limits under JOB-09, with skipped inference overlap under JOB-08 and visible failure policy. Provide create/edit, enable/disable, Run now, inspect and cancel controls. Each run has a linked agent transcript, tool/action history, usage, outcome and created work/artifacts. Persist discovery checkpoints and action identities so repeated issue scans and retries do not duplicate actions. Unresolved actions enter the existing input queue with notifications. Apply no-server and pause/exit constraints, with automatic schedule/run resumption and no catch-up under JOB-03–04; reconcile external effects before retry.

The agent launched by a scheduled inference task has the full configured tool access available to an authorized coordinator/implementation agent, including tools that select and start work. It is not restricted to monitoring or read-only actions merely because it was scheduled. It may call next_work(project, feature = null) to select a feature or standalone issue, or pass a feature to select one of its tasks, and start that work. Existing tool permissions, plan-readiness/approval rules and explicit pauses still apply; scheduled execution does not grant a policy bypass.

If a scheduled inference task is still running when its next scheduled occurrence arrives, skip that occurrence. Do not start an overlapping run or queue that occurrence for later catch-up. Preserve the current run and expose the skipped outcome in schedule history. Existing restart, interruption and explicit-pause rules remain in effect.

Scheduled inference jobs report per-run usage and costs but have no job spending limits or monetary-limit holds. Apply ROUTE-17 reported/estimated/free/untracked classifications. Feature work started by a schedule remains subject to that feature’s configured budget and normal approval, pause, eligibility and permission rules; invoking it through a job must not bypass those controls. Ordinary cancellation, deadlines and resource controls remain independent of monetary limits.

Retained CodeGraph operations must be manually invokable in the app. The user must not need to ask an agent or run the old service to perform them. Manual and scheduled invocation must use the same validated operations as agents where applicable.

Inventory the retained operations and jobs before implementation scope is frozen. Candidate operations include repository discovery/indexing/reindexing, schema sync, selected analysis, graph linking/community detection, embeddings, and maintenance. Show prerequisites, target scope, progress, cancellation, actual outcome, and recovery actions.
Indexing logs must be visible, including enough detail to diagnose failures. Repository, database-schema, and optional semantic indexing must not hide their errors behind a generic failed badge.

A run’s diagnostics must correlate operation, target, stage, source revision, attempt, timestamps, progress, warnings/errors, helper output where relevant, and error classification. Provide filtering/search, live inspection, retained run history, copy/export, and links to safe recovery actions while redacting credentials and controlling large output.

Partial indexing, stale data, cancelled runs, and terminal or retryable failures must be distinguishable. Logs and relevant artifacts must survive restart under a defined retention policy. Jobs run while the application is open, including while other screens are active. Closing the main window pauses work and exits. Feature and issue work require manual selection after closing and reopening; it continues automatically after sleep while the app remains open. Enabled maintenance/inference schedules reactivate automatically; missed occurrences stay skipped and interrupted runs resume automatically. Detailed recovery mechanics still need policy.

Indexed CodeGraph references confirm job types for repository discovery, community detection, convention embedding ingestion, and assistant retention cleanup. The route map also exposes schedules, manual operations, schemas and graph exploration. These references establish a starting inventory, not proof that every retained job or new target adapter is already ported.

Start with fresh repository indexing rather than migrating the existing derived code index. Import existing CodeGraph projects, features, tasks and their histories. This is the complete selected migration scope; exclude existing memory, knowledge, lessons and conventions. Preserve the imported records and their historical relationships when rebuilding indexes. The exclusion concerns migration only; the new harness still provides its required Knowledge and convention management capabilities.

Inventory all records and relationships within the selected project, feature, task and history scope: repository associations, plans, priorities, statuses, dependencies, agent/session and transcript links, decisions and Git/PR/review history, with referenced evidence where present. Preserve source identities or durable ID mappings, attribution, timestamps and provenance. Use a consistent read-only snapshot/export, validate counts and links, and make import resumable without duplicates. Report missing data or mapping failures rather than silently dropping selected records. Preserve historical code references while reconciling links to fresh indexes. Import must not automatically resume old agents, execute queued effects or treat historical checks as current verification.

A watcher lets a session start background work or a wait and be woken when it ends, without holding a turn open. These requirements restate the agreed watcher behavior of 4 November 2026 from the implemented watch service.

An agent must be able to start a long-running process, such as a build, a test run or a dev server, as a watcher and keep working. Creating a watcher launches the process through the same process-execution service as a plain run, with the same registered executables, working roots, shell safety checks, and time and output limits, and returns the watcher before the process exits.

Watchers must be listed, inspected and cancelled through the same operations for the UI and for agents. Inspection shows the watcher state, elapsed time, match count and the current redacted output tail. Cancel can stop the process the watcher launched, or only stop observing it. Stopping observation leaves the process running under its owner and reports nothing.

When a watcher settles, DevWorks must deliver what it observed once, to the session that created the watcher, as a host-authored message. Delivery must survive a restart. The message counts as handled only when a turn that carried it completes. Agents and add-ons cannot write watcher messages.

A watcher outcome reports only what was observed: Succeeded, Failed, TimedOut, Cancelled, Interrupted, Lost or Uncertain, with the exit code or signal, the duration and the redacted output tail. Starting a process, or polling one, is never reported as success.

A watcher may poll instead of waiting on one process. A probe runs a command at an interval, waiting twice as long after each run that fails the condition, up to eight intervals, until a run meets it: an exit code (0 by default) and optionally an output pattern. The watcher then settles Succeeded with the run count. A run that cannot launch, or is lost or uncertain, ends the watcher with that outcome.

A watcher may be a timer that fires at a stated time or after a stated delay, settles Succeeded and wakes the session. A timer launches nothing, so every role may create and cancel one, including a read-only reviewer.

A watcher lives as long as its owner. When the owning session ends, or its project is archived or deleted, the watcher is cancelled and the process it launched is stopped, and nothing is delivered. While the owner is paused or held, events wait and are delivered in order after Continue.

Watchers must be honest across shutdown and restart. At an orderly shutdown, a watched process that DevWorks stopped settles Interrupted, and a probe forgets the stopped run and runs again after reopen once the owner continues. A timer that came due while the app was closed fires once. After a crash, a process killed by boot recovery is reported Interrupted.

A watcher may count regular-expression matches in a process output as it streams, or in the lines of a file it watches. By default it completes on the first match. In each-match mode it reports matches in coalesced wakes, at most one per minimum interval (30 seconds by default), each carrying its count, so a burst of matches cannot flood the session and the final count still includes every match.

Launching or stopping a process through a watcher needs everything the process tools require: the process tool family, a role that is not read-only, the shell-tools setting, the shell safety checks (at creation as well as at launch) and, under Project scope, a native-execution exception. A watcher that only observes, such as a timer, needs none of these.

Every polling or file watcher must end. It has a maximum lifetime, set on the watcher or taken from the watch.maxLifetimeMs setting (24 hours by default, inherited from workspace to project), and it settles TimedOut when the lifetime passes, stopping a run in flight.

A backup check must catch what primary delivery missed. When watch.backupEnabled is on (the default) and at least every watch.backupIntervalMs (15 minutes by default, at least 1 minute), it settles an outcome the primary pass never settled, marks Lost a recorded process the operating system reports gone, reminds the owner of a probe that has not run for more than twice its interval or whose source status cannot be established, and delivers pending events with their own IDs. Each such delivery is recorded as a missed primary delivery in history and diagnostics.

Do not port or bundle CodeGraph’s legacy Shortcut or RabbitMQ integrations into DevWorks. Neither service may become a core application dependency. Preserve general outgoing MCP client support and the user-requested incoming DevWorks MCP server under MCP-01/07. Imported work/history may retain historical source references without requiring a live legacy connector. Internal asynchronous delivery uses the native application/runtime and durable persistence contracts rather than RabbitMQ.

title: 22 Architecture resolution and implementation acceptance
intro: Architecture baseline 1.1 is complete as of 2 November 2026. Product choices are captured; Proposed requirements retain their status. The former interview questions are retained historically in requirements-interview.json. The register below names implementation acceptance, not unresolved architecture. Use the local implementation plan for exact ownership and dependencies.
blocks: Adopted design and remaining implementation acceptance

Storage. SQLite graph tables, FTS5 and sqlite-vec with core-owned repository/transaction contracts are adopted. Qualify actual persistence, claims, snapshots, migration/manual restore, publication and target durability.

Native UI. Native egui/eframe and service-owned projections are adopted, including shared Home/sidebar identity and semantic widget contracts. Qualify full panes, streaming, keyboard, OS accessibility, native attachments and clean target installations.

Providers. Retain native router/profile contracts, Codex and opt-in direct simple-router Claude subscription; add a distinct Anthropic API key and billing profile. The user accepts the unsupported subscription risk explicitly. Qualify auth, refresh/revocation, risk admission, media/tools/cache/usage, SystemOne and actual endpoint compatibility. No external coding CLI is adopted.

Enforcement. Full default, verified reviewer reads, host authority/revocation, dedicated repository deletion and fail-closed restricted admission are adopted. Qualify actual destructive/credential/outbound/process/confinement races and each target.

Extensions. Framed native host/SDK contracts, all eight contribution types, signed trust, scoped callbacks, quiescent registry/state publication and guarded rollback are adopted. Qualify actual interoperability, authority, failure recovery and target packaging.

Scope and retrieval. Exact source views, overlay masking, current scope filtering, immutable source citations, retained document versions and checked publication are adopted. Qualify complete cross-repository/rename/delete/uncommitted behavior and reference-aware cleanup.

Git and delivery. All-repository readiness, ordered non-atomic delivery, uncertain-outcome reconciliation and guarded owned cleanup are adopted. Qualify actual GitHub rules/queues, all merge methods, conflicts, review evidence and release/deployment approvals.

Documents and databases. Modern .docx, Markdown/text and pinned native PDF candidates are selected. Relational targets are SQLite, MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server. HelixDB schema reading is removed; DW-038 is retired. Qualify format/metadata/read-only coverage and source retention.

Automation. Owned native browser/CDP, explicit desktop capability/OK-Wait consent and optional container ownership are adopted. Qualify full retained controls, private transport, permission/display differences and lifecycle.

Distribution and recovery. Target matrix, offline Help, native credentials, separate managed roots, manual backup/restore and approved signed app updates are adopted. Qualify installers, runtime absence, signing, path moves and recovery on each supported target.

Retained scope. The 353 requirements and all 353 operations/48 families have owners and candidate contracts. The 63 active local slices cover 494 retained source entries, 64 audited exclusions and 33 acceptance groups. Qualify actual services/source semantics, import and drift.

Performance. Twelve workload specifications and provisional engineering budgets exist. Measure actual native process trees, startup/idle/index/query/transcript/queue and installer footprint on named target hardware; do not claim unexecuted measurements.

title: 23 End to end acceptance scenarios
intro: These scenarios define observable outcomes for the eventual implementation. They are review criteria, not claims that the prototype implements the system. Detailed tests must be derived from the approved requirements and risk of each slice.
blocks: A base install opens workspace chat on each target OS. Navigation is left, active conversation center, searchable session history right, with no conversation dropdown or mandatory framework/runtime setup. DEC 01–09; UI 01–05; PLAT 01–03.
A project containing three repositories supports a feature spanning two of them. Each repository keeps its own revisions, worktrees, checks, and PRs. MODEL 01–03; WORK 01–07; GIT 01–05.

A human creates and prioritizes a feature, creates and moves cards, and an agent performs the equivalent operations. Both paths enforce the same rules and show attributed history; a stale edit preserves the draft. ARCH 02; WORK 01–07.

Start creates/selects the coordinator and reviews the existing plan. A ready authorized plan proceeds; incomplete planning produces a candidate plan and approval/input request before unapproved work. Pause is acknowledged; Start on paused work through the UI, an agent or a schedule leaves it paused and requests explicit Continue. Agents and schedules cannot Continue human-paused work without explicit user authorization; allowing new starts is insufficient. Authorized Continue preserves current state and lineage without duplicate ownership, lost artifacts or bypassing unresolved holds. Continue feature/issue resumes its coordinator and eligible descendants, including nested assignments, while child-specific blockers remain effective; manual child pauses are not supported. AGENT 01–09, 12; CONTROL 01–07, 12–13.
The workspace coordinator answers a question about a feature, PR, active agents, or required input using current records, with links and explicit uncertainty where applicable. COORD 01–08.

The user inspects a worker transcript and tool activity, changes direction, and sees acknowledgment and plan reconciliation. Late old-plan results do not overwrite current instructions. CONTROL 01–07; CONTEXT 01–03.

Opening a completed or paused feature reveals its coordinator lineage, workers, transcript sessions, Git changes, reviews, PRs, verification evidence, decisions, and failures. HISTORY 01–02; GIT 01–05.

On a clean installation, baseline structural indexing works without optional .NET, Node, Swift or Rust toolchains. Use Settings Add-ons to install prebuilt .NET, TypeScript, Swift and Rust semantic packs without rebuilding the host or requiring a compiler merely to install the pack. With declared project prerequisites available, validate each pack against a representative project and its claimed capabilities, including Swift native index-store adaptation and SCIP imports. Inspect versions, compatibility, configuration, project enablement and diagnostics; test update, disable and uninstall. Missing/incompatible dependencies, helper failure, cancellation and stale/mismatched output remain visible, preserve baseline indexing and do not block unrelated work. Verify process cleanup and worktree/revision provenance. CODE 01–11; ADDON 01–04; SET 01–02; LOG 01–03.

An exhausted or failing provider creates a visible wait or bounded fallback under policy. All inference remains routed; request attribution, reported/estimated/unknown costs, and partial response recovery remain correct. ROUTE 01–08.

Off tracks spend without a cap. Configure a limit: coordinator warnings begin at 75%, with remaining-budget information; at the limit, further inference pauses. Raise the limit or switch it Off: work stays paused until manual Continue, which still honors other blockers and limits. Verify shared coordinator/worker/review attribution and concurrent calls without invented prices for unknown-cost routes. Retain incurred usage; required checks and acceptance still govern completion. ROUTE 06–08, 11; AGENT 07, 13.

Create memory, knowledge and lesson items in one workspace; tag, search, filter and edit them manually and through agent tools. Verify shared identity/history and retained evidence and lesson metadata, without duplicate catalogs. Changing category tags must not change project/shared scope. KNOW 01–08.

Record a general lesson in one project and verify automatic availability to another project with its origin and applicability retained. Record project-specific knowledge and a convention; verify that another project does not receive them through retrieval, context assembly or dreaming consolidation. KNOW 04, 07; CONTEXT 01; CONV 01–02.

Contradictory evidence creates a review item without erasing either source. Only affected work waits. A reasoned resolution checks current revisions and is linked to the work; reading a notification alone changes no decision. KNOW 01–06; REVIEW 01–03; NOTIFY 01–03.

A run automatically applies non-conflicting consolidation without per-change approval, preserves scope and records instructions, usage, changes and outcome. Unresolved conflicts enter the review queue and notify the user while independent consolidation continues. A later edit causes a revert conflict rather than an overwrite. DREAM 01–05; KNOW 07; REVIEW 01; NOTIFY 01.

Interrupt a push, merge, database mutation and tool operation before execution and after an effect but before local acknowledgment. Reconcile outcomes before retry; never repeat completed effects. Unresolved outcomes hold affected/dependent work and notify the user; unrelated work continues. Crash after activation commit but before launch: pending feature/issue work stays paused after reopening until selective explicit Continue. Preserve other holds. Trigger manual backup/restore; verify no automatic backups run. STORE 01–07; CONTROL 05–07, 10; OPS 01–02.

Long transcripts, large backlogs, indexing, concurrent agents, and resized panes meet agreed targets without a blocked UI or hidden resource runaway. Accessibility and offline management remain usable. UI 06–07; PERF 01–02; SEC 01–02.

Configure different custom columns and status names in two projects. Rename and reorder columns through UI and tools; each project retains its own workflow. Verify that status identities and history survive renaming and that allocation uses explicit readiness/completion semantics. Removing an occupied status requires explicit reassignment without lost work. Board movement must not clear execution holds or bypass approvals, reviews, checks or merge policy. WORK 02–03, 13–14; MODEL 03; WORK 09–10.

With no webhook endpoint or relay, detect remote pushes, PR merges, issue updates, reviews and check changes through direct API polling. Verify attributed application events reach relevant agent sessions and code-affecting events refresh the correct configured ref/revision with visible index freshness. Issue/review-only changes do not reindex code. Exercise conditional responses, rate-limit backoff, duplicate polls, restart and offline/sleep recovery; notification and indexing delivery remain independent and traceable. Preserve manual work pauses and skipped scheduled runs. GH 10–12; CODE 04–05; CONTROL 08–11; JOB 03–04.

Connect a repository with existing open GitHub issues and verify automatic import into the project issue list. Then report a new issue and verify automatic import without a manual action or inference schedule. Preserve the source owner/repository, remote identity and clickable link; repeated discovery, offline recovery and restart must reuse the same local issue. Verify inbound updates and one verified-resolution summary/close without publishing intermediate local tracking. Check the configurable app-wide 30-minute default admission gate, persisted pacing across restart, shared-repository triage routing, immediate eligible work on verified bugs and notifications for feature requests/unverifiable bugs. Preserve existing pauses and deduplicate observations. GH 05–09; WORK 09–11.

Create a local issue and verify creation/editing stays local. Explicitly publish or link it and verify inbound GitHub updates, same-bug clarification and new-scope decisions. Keep intermediate execution details local; only verified completion posts a resolution summary and closes remotely. Test offline/restart recovery, deduplicated uncertain comment/close outcomes, conflicting edits, authentication/rate-limit errors and visible retry state. Remote closure must preserve verified started fixes and approved feature work; retain feature requests for manual choice. Preserve independent pauses, attribution, source links and unresolved conflict evidence. GH 03–09; WORK 13–14; CONTROL 08–10.

Create a project-level issue without a feature through UI and agent tools. Find and prioritize it, then start implementation immediately without a synthetic feature or separate plan approval. Verify that unclear requirements request input while existing tool, user-pause, review and Auto-Merge policies remain effective under AGENT-15. Verify attributed usage/cost tracking without an issue spending cap, 75% budget warning or budget-triggered pause under ROUTE-12. Delegate scoped work to subagents without creating a feature. Inspect parent/child agent lineage, execution transcripts, worktree/branch/PR links, review/fix/check results, activity and artifacts on the issue; verify shared permissions, isolation and pause/redirect controls under AGENT-14. Verify the independent per-issue concurrency default of 10, a changed cap and useful parallel delegation within that cap without a global agent-count limit under AGENT-10–11. A feature link remains optional. Verify its PR targets main, apply review/fix/check and Auto-Merge policy, and exercise pause/continue and reviewer write restrictions. Verify automatic cleanup of harness-owned worktrees and local branches after confirmed merge to main, preserving transcripts, artifacts, GitHub links and complete history. Unintegrated work must survive; cleanup failure must be visible and retryable. WORK 03, 11–12; GIT 02–05, 10–12; TOOL 05.

Create prioritized features with child tasks and standalone issues. next_work(project) and explicit feature=null select the highest-priority eligible feature or standalone issue from one project queue. Verify either kind can win by priority and feature child tasks cannot bypass their feature. next_work(project, feature) selects only that feature’s tasks. Reject wrong-project features and expose empty/blocked outcomes. Concurrent scheduled/coordinator callers and retries must not duplicate assignments or starts. Skip incomplete/unapproved features and select only features approved for implementation; preserve clear actionable issue eligibility. Honor pauses, dependencies, budgets and current approval. Verify a scheduled agent can use the same enabled tools to allocate/start work with coordinator/worker lineage and schedule provenance. WORK 09–10; JOB 07; AGENT 01–13; TOOL 01–05.

Create app/project inference schedules. Run a GitHub issue monitor through the router and permitted tools; inspect transcript, usage, actions and created work. Repeat scans/retries without duplicate effects; test scope, disabled/unavailable tools, approval, notifications, cancellation and failure. Close the app: work stops. Reopen: enabled schedules reactivate, missed occurrences stay skipped and interrupted runs resume with their history. Preserve independent holds; feature and issue agents remain paused until manual Continue. Verify an occurrence arriving during an active inference run is skipped, with no overlapping run or catch-up. JOB 01–08; ROUTE 01; TOOL 01–05; GH 04.

Index schema without row-content indexing. Verify new connections default to read-only and reject mutations. Explicitly enable writes on one connection: exercise permitted inserts/updates/deletes through data tools while another connection stays read-only and disabled tools stay denied. Disable writes: direct and indirect mutations are refused while authorized reads remain available. Verify reviewer write denial even when other agents can write. Inspect connection/scope, attributed results and failures. Apply a schema change through a committed migration; when migrations are not possible, exercise a direct schema change and inspect its history. Verify both paths reject application to read-only connections or by reviewers, and a commit alone grants no execution authority. Share one connection across two projects with different access; verify enforcement and attribution, rejection of an unauthorized third project, and no write elevation over read-only connection settings. Schema indexing remains read-only. DB 01–09; TOOL 01–05; LOG 01–03.

Open tasks with individual and grouped PRs, including a task spanning repositories. Verify task-visible repository identities, current worktree paths, branches and PR links, with navigation to agent history and inspectable changes/checks/reviews. Each task covered by a grouped PR links to it. After cleanup, retain history while marking removed resources accurately. Manual staging/commit/branch/merge controls are not required; autonomous Git delivery remains available under configured policy. GIT 01–10; HISTORY 01–02.

Import CodeGraph projects, features, tasks and their histories; rebuild repository indexes from source. Compare selected source/target records, identities/mappings, statuses, dependencies and history/evidence links. Verify that memory, knowledge, lessons and conventions are not imported. Repeat after interruption without duplicates or silent omissions. Historical code references remain inspectable while fresh index links reconcile. Imported work does not start executing automatically. Missing source data or mapping failures are reported. IMPORT 01–02; MODEL 02; STORE 05–06.

Work in a repository with AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md plus subdirectory instructions. Verify automatic loading and the applicable directory scope, including work spanning paths/repositories. Verify that the files supplement role instructions, an explicit user direction takes precedence and a file cannot enable a disabled tool or grant reviewer writes. Retain instruction-source revisions in session context history. CONTEXT 02–03, 06; TOOL 02–05.

Drive an active agent to 80% of the routed model context limit and verify automatic compaction and continued work without user input. Retain the full original transcript, logical agent identity, work links and compaction history. Verify retained instructions, plan, unresolved decisions and artifact references. Exercise changed model limits, oversized tool results and compaction failure with visible bounded recovery. CONTEXT 01–05; ROUTE 01.

Compare successive provider requests through text and parallel tool turns, including built-in and MCP definitions, retries and restart. Verify unchanged eligible prefixes, stable content boundaries, tool IDs and required continuation blocks. Exercise instruction/permission changes, model/upstream fallback and compaction: apply required changes and explain reduced reuse without weakening correctness. On supported endpoints inspect actual cached/uncached/write usage and total cost; unavailable metrics remain explicit. Local prefix checks must not claim a guaranteed provider hit. CACHE 01–06; ROUTE 01–10; CONTEXT 04–05.

Have an agent save a screenshot and report, another agent discover/read them by stable reference, and the user preview, attach and export them. Add a file through the UI and expose it through agent tools. Verify explicit originating project, feature and task links, navigation in both directions, and preservation of origin when another task reuses the artifact. Verify scope, provenance, versions and persistence after restart and worktree cleanup. Verify that age and storage pressure do not cause default deletion; retained artifacts remain until an explicit delete operation. Exercise read-only reviewer access and a storage failure. ART 01–05; GIT 06–07; STORE 05–06.

With the app unfocused, create an item requiring user input and verify a native OS notification where supported and permitted. Deny permission or suppress OS alerts and verify the in-app notification and approval item remain available. Reading/dismissing an alert does not resolve the decision or resume paused work. Validate macOS, Windows and supported Linux desktop environments. NOTIFY 01–04; REVIEW 01–03.

With user activity present, request native UI control and verify the OK/Wait prompt. Until answered, and after Wait, no automation input or focus takeover occurs; independent tasks continue. After OK and resource allocation, run the authorized operation. A resource grant alone must not substitute for consent. UIQA 04–05; RES 01–03; NOTIFY 01.

Have tasks in different projects request the same desktop resource at capacity one; grant one and visibly queue the other while independent tasks continue. Inspect holder, purpose and priority; renew and release through tools. Verify retry idempotency, stale-owner rejection and recovery before reassignment after expiry. Exercise a capacity greater than one on another resource. RES 01–03; UIQA 04; AGENT 09–11.

Use browser control to exercise a website and native control to exercise a desktop app; inspect linked actions, assertions, screenshots, logs and tested revision. Exercise missing permissions and unsupported controls. Verify browser session isolation, desktop input coordinated by resource reservations, interruption and reviewer write denial. Validate backend provisioning without preinstalled application runtimes. UIQA 01–05; RES 01–03; TOOL 05; PLAT 01–03.

Start incomplete planning: the coordinator plans what it can and requests approval/input before unapproved execution. A ready authorized plan proceeds without redundant approval. Refine through UI and chat before/during execution; verify visible changes, retained history, reconciliation and rejection of stale results. Task breakdown, delegation, sequencing and PR grouping may change autonomously within approved requirements and policies. Propose changed scope or acceptance criteria: require explicit user approval before executing that change while valid unblocked work continues. Verify both approval and rejection outcomes, and correctness evidence. AGENT 12–13; WORK 08; CONTROL 01–04.

Close the main window with multiple features and issues active; verify pause/save/exit. Reopen into workspace chat with their agents paused. Resume selected features and issues together and verify that unselected work and unresolved blocked tasks do not start. CONTROL 08–10; REVIEW 03.

With the app open and feature and issue agents, maintenance and inference jobs running, sleep and wake the computer; eligible work continues automatically, while existing user pauses and blockers remain. Close and reopen to verify that features and issues instead require manual selection. Verify keep-awake defaults to off on all three platforms. Enable it for an idle open app; verify the display may turn off while work continues, and release on disable/exit. CONTROL 08–11; POWER 01–02; JOB 03–04.

With independent ready tasks and capacity available, run multiple tasks simultaneously in distinct task worktrees and refill completed slots up to the per-feature cap. Verify coordinator integration also uses a worktree, the primary checkout is unchanged, and task/worktree history remains linked. Verify the default of 10, a changed cap, independent allowances for simultaneously active features without a global agent-count cap, and continued progress while another task waits for user input. AGENT 09–11; GIT 02; REVIEW 03.

Run several tasks for a multi-repository feature in isolated worktrees. Have the coordinator group related tasks into one PR and use another PR for separate work; all target their repository feature branches. Verify no PR to main is opened before feature implementation completion. Then open final feature PRs to main, retain task/group PR lineage, and enforce review/fix/check and Auto-Merge policies. Keep required resources during pending delivery and perform cleanup after verified integration. GIT 02, 06–09; DELIVERY 01–08.

After verified final delivery of a multi-repository feature, verify automatic removal of all its harness-created task/integration worktrees and local branches. Confirm that commits, transcripts, PR/review links and historical ownership remain browsable, and unrelated user resources remain intact. Exercise a cleanup failure and verify visible status and retry without data loss. GIT 02, 06–07, 09; HISTORY 01–02.

Configure Codex sign-in, optional direct Claude subscription sign-in with explicit risk acceptance, a separate Anthropic API-key connection, OpenRouter credentials, and local/remote OpenAI-compatible endpoints, including Ollama and LM Studio. Verify separate credentials, route eligibility and billing; no implicit subscription/API switch. Exercise supported discovery, connection testing, refresh, reauthentication and disconnect. Verify that chat, workers, reviews, dreaming, embeddings, context summaries/titles and accepted MCP inference use the internal router with attributed usage and visible failures. ROUTE 01–11; MCP 05.

Have an implementation agent install a project dependency within authorized scope without an approval prompt. Request a system-wide tool/package installation; verify execution waits for user approval and denial prevents installation. Verify disabled tools and reviewer read-only restrictions still apply, with attributable installation and approval history. TOOL 05–07; CONTROL 01–07.

Have the harness propose an improvement to its Rust code, plan it as project work, and execute the approved scope in isolated worktrees through implementation, checks, PR review/fixes and configured delivery. Verify permissions, plan approval, required reviews and merge policy remain effective. Verify documentation is included in the plan and delivered changes; an implementation with missing or stale required Help/developer documentation must fail completion and delivery review. Inspect linked transcripts, Git/review history, documentation changes, build artifacts and evidence. Distinguish merged/tested source from the running app. Pending or denied installation/restart approval leaves the installed version running; PR merge alone must not activate a build. Approve an update: verify recorded approval/outcomes, safe shutdown and selective manual feature/issue resume. SELF 01–04; HELP 02–06; AGENT 12–13; GIT 02, 08–10; DELIVERY 01–08; CONTROL 08–10.

Create two worktrees with different committed and uncommitted changes, including staged edits, an indexable untracked file, deletion and rename. Verify each agent automatically queries its own view across search, source, traversal, impact and context tools; main and the other worktree remain unchanged. Check explicit cross-view inspection, revision/local-snapshot provenance, confidence and unresolved relationships. Move the baseline and edit during indexing: reject stale or mixed snapshots and report rebuild progress. Exercise request reuse, missing/failed/expired views and retries. Cleanup retires derived views without deleting history or artifacts. Baseline-only analysis and unavailable semantic coverage must remain explicit. CODE 05–11; GIT 02, 06–07; LOG 01–03.
Chat model selector and session pinning

In every composer, choose a router model and verify it persists until changed. Select Auto; verify the pin survives turns, tools, compaction and app restarts. Rate-limit or disable the pinned model: automatically switch to an eligible available replacement and retain its pin after restart and original-model recovery. Restoring pins must not resume paused features/issues. Sessions remain independent, routed and attributed. Verify capability/permission constraints and attachment retention. With all eligible models cooling, verify no early retries, automatic reconnection at the earliest expiry and updated cooldown handling; unrelated holds remain. Missing retry times and capability changes await review. UI 02, 10; ROUTE 01–05, 13–15.

In every chat composer, attach images and files using the selection dialog, drag-and-drop and paste. Verify correct message/session association, retained files and applicable work/artifact links after switching chats, restart and compaction. Ask an agent to inspect a screenshot/image artifact; verify a vision-capable model/endpoint is selected through the router and visual content reaches it. Exercise unavailable vision routes and unsupported/failed file processing with visible outcomes and no false analysis claim. UI 02–04, 08–09; ROUTE 01, 13; ART 01–05; CONTEXT 04–05.

Verify web search and page fetching work as built-in tools without an external MCP server and are enabled by default. Exercise coordinator, implementation and read-only review access, source URLs, recorded results and work attribution. Disable each tool in Settings and verify invocation is denied. Backend selection, configuration and result-handling details follow the selected implementation contract. TOOL 01–05, 08; HISTORY 01–02.

Verify implementation agents have shell/process tools enabled by default; disable them and verify denial at invocation. Connect to an external MCP server as a client; verify read-only tools start enabled. Connect an independent harness to the DevWorks MCP server and retrieve indexed code, planned work and Knowledge with citations and scope isolation; verify default write denial, explicit work/Knowledge grants, revocation, receipt recovery and app-close unavailability across stdio and HTTP. Change individual toggles and use Select all; verify the effective agent tool set matches the saved selection and invocations retain attribution. Verify the shared selection across coordinator, coding and review agents, including the same selected read tools. Verify that reviewer mutations through built-in, MCP and shell/process tools are refused by the harness even after Select all; findings are retained and fixes go to an authorized implementation agent. Disabled tools are refused at invocation, saved choices survive discovery, and an unavailable server affects only dependent work. MCP 01–11; TOOL 01–06; SET 01–02.

Verify Auto-Merge and mandatory independent review both start enabled. Test project and repository overrides independently for each setting, with repository overrides taking precedence and effective values and sources visible. With mandatory review enabled, verify configured GitHub automated reviews satisfy the gate without a duplicate reviewer while automation is working; failed or stalled automation uses an independent in-app fallback. For a repository without automated reviews configured, verify a separate in-app reviewer and fix cycle. In both cases, required reviews must complete and all actionable findings must be resolved before merge. Auto-Merge off stops before merge; Auto-Merge on still cannot merge with any unresolved actionable finding. Verify the default limit of 3 fix cycles, a changed limit, and escalation plus notification when the coordinator cannot reach a decision. Unblocked feature tasks continue while the affected task waits; feature-wide waiting requires a dependency that blocks the remaining work. DELIVERY 01–08; REVIEW 03.

Configure deployment and release-publishing policies independently at workspace, project and repository levels. Verify both default to Ask me, inherited values and override sources are visible, and Auto-Merge does not authorize either action. Test approval and rejection for Ask me, refusal for Disabled, and permitted automatic actions under existing tool permissions. Different repositories and the two action types retain independent policies. A self-improvement build still requires installation/restart approval. DELIVERY 01, 04, 09; SELF 01–03; TOOL 01–05; REVIEW 01–03.

Connect one GitHub.com account; discover personal and organization repositories. Associate repositories from different owners with a project and inspect authorization and PR/check/review state. Verify authorized organization delivery and visible permission denial. Across chat, tasks, histories and notifications, every referenced GitHub resource is a clickable link to the correct owner/repository resource. Edit active role instructions: persist and adopt at the next safe step without restart. Have an agent propose a revision: pending/rejected changes must not affect active instructions; approved changes adopt at the next safe step. Inspect history and rollback, retaining reviewer write denial. Navigate Settings without losing chat. GH 01–04; SET 01–06; TOOL 05.

For SQLite, MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, configure a source, index its supported schema, navigate objects and relationships, inspect freshness, and remove indexed metadata without changing the source. Verify each engine independently, including read tools and permitted writes versus denied writes. Report adapter/version coverage. Reject unsupported HelixDB source configuration. Use distinctive source values and verify that only schema metadata persists, with no records/property values in indexing results, logs, transcripts, artifacts, caches or embeddings, including failure paths. From a repository home, traverse Overview/Nodes/Health/Reviews, internal code-project and node-type drill-down, container/member lists, node details, source and incoming/outgoing cross-repository links; verify repository breadcrumbs and return context. DB 01–07; SCHEMA 01–02; GRAPH 01–04.

Run a manual operation and a scheduled job. Inspect logs for partial or failed indexing, retry safely, and distinguish repository health findings from app service health. Review code findings against the correct revision. After reopening, verify enabled schedules use future due times with no catch-up for missed occurrences; interrupted maintenance/inference runs resume automatically while feature and issue agents remain paused. JOB 01–06; OP 01–02; LOG 01–03; HEALTH 01–02; CODEREVIEW 01–02.

Discover an existing shared skill from ~/.agents/skills and create a harness-specific skill in the dedicated directory. Verify that both are manageable and show their origin/path. For same-name skills, verify that the harness-specific version is active and the shared file remains intact. Select scope and enabled state, then verify that a relevant agent receives the correct versions under its effective tool policy. Edit a skill during active work and verify adoption at the next safe step, with the version transition in session history. Load a skill’s referenced document and asset, then run an authorized helper script. Verify disabled-tool enforcement, project scope, reviewer read-only restrictions and system-install approval; missing optional runtimes must be visible without preventing core app use. Have an agent propose a new harness-specific skill and an edit: neither may alter active skills or become available before approval. Reject one, approve another; inspect agent/work attribution, rationale, reviewed revisions, outcomes and safe-step adoption. Propose an override of a shared skill: pending/rejected versions leave selection unchanged; approval activates the harness override at the next safe step. Verify shared originals stay untouched and source/override provenance is retained. Exercise proposed stale-approval reconciliation and rollback; distinguish validation from claimed effectiveness. Also create or import a convention. CONV 01–02; SKILL 01–09; TOOL 02–07; PLAT 03.

Ask an agent to build a package with a custom tool, command, event-driven verification step, context contribution and native findings panel. Verify development/test evidence and version-bound approval: reject one version, approve another, and confirm only the approved contents activate at a safe boundary without rebuilding the host. Manage language packs and harness packages in one Add-ons screen. Verify scope, requested/effective access, configuration, enable/disable/update/uninstall, package state and version attribution after restart, and guarded rollback. Exercise hook failure, cancellation and recovery without duplicate external effects or stalled unrelated work. Package host calls must preserve router use, read-only reviewer restrictions, required review gates, transcript history and context/cache rules. Prebuilt installation does not require a compiler or a TypeScript runtime. Existing Pi/Oh My Pi packages must not be presented as compatible without a separately validated adapter. EXT 01–06; ADDON 01–04; TOOL 01–05; ROUTE 01; CACHE 01–06; CONTEXT 04–06; SET 05–06; SKILL 07–09.

Rebase an agent-owned task branch and verify an automatic guarded force-push is permitted. Request a feature-branch force-push: it waits for explicit approval bound to the concrete operation; rejection leaves the ref unchanged. Verify another agent or user branch receives no automatic task-branch authority. Attempt a forced main update through flags, forced refspecs and equivalent harness-dispatched forms: always reject it regardless of Auto-Merge or approval for another action. Changed remote revisions fail the expected-revision check and require reconciliation. Repository protections remain in force. Inspect task/feature, agent, approval and Git outcome history. GIT 02, 10, 13–14; DELIVERY 01, 04; TOOL 01–05; EXT 04.

Prepare final feature PRs in three repositories with a dependency chain. Leave one required check or review pending or failing: verify no final PR merges, including ready PRs in other repositories. Make every final PR pass its required checks and reviews, resolve all actionable findings, and verify merges follow dependency order while honoring each repository’s Auto-Merge and approval policy. Inspect per-repository outcomes and linked feature delivery history. After an earlier repository merges, introduce a routine conflict in a later one, including changes from another concurrent agent: verify autonomous resolution and continuation, with renewed checks/reviews for the changed revision and no user notification. Exercise an unusual failure the coordinator cannot resolve: pause only affected delivery and dependent work, notify with evidence, and keep independent work running. Do not bypass review gates or force-push main. GIT 04–05, 08–10, 13, 15–16; DELIVERY 01–08.

Merge final feature PRs across affected repositories: keep the feature incomplete while any final PR is unmerged, then mark it complete once all merges are verified. Leave a linked release or deployment pending, awaiting approval or failed: the merged feature stays complete, with separate release/deployment statuses and links to the relevant repositories, revisions and history. Confirm separate release/deployment authority is preserved. Verify feature worktree/local-branch cleanup and visible cleanup outcomes, retaining history and artifacts. GIT 06–10, 15–17; DELIVERY 09; ART 01–05.

Create a project: keep-working is off by default. Explicitly enable it with several eligible features and standalone issues: run only one work item at a time per project, then automatically select/start the next by priority after completion. Verify internal subagent concurrency remains available and two projects can work independently. Automatic selection skips incomplete or unapproved features; explicit Start may separately develop a plan and request approval. Pauses, budgets, permissions, resources, ownership and manual-resume holds remain effective. After closing/reopening, keep-working stays stopped until manually restarted.
